subsubtopic: CALL FOR ACTION ON INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the day before yesterday I brought a motion before this House regarding the injurious effects of high interest rates on the canning industry in Prince Edward County. These same rates have now forced a major Ontario apple packer into receivership and are affecting apple growers in this same county. Perhaps this double blow will bring the government to the realization that the primary resource of Canada, food, is in jeopardy.
I again move, seconded by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees):
That the Minister of Finance immediately institute reasonable interest rates for small business, particularly those involved in agriculture.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MEETING OF FIRST MINISTERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the fact the government has now frittered away an entire year of its mandate picking political fights with the provinces and with millions of Canadians over constitutional and energy matters, while allowing the economy of Canada to deteriorate to its worst state since the great depression, I move, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, and seconded by the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid):
That the federal government agree to stop-to stop here and now-its antagonistic, unilateral attack on the constitutional rights of the provinces so that an emergency meeting of first ministers might be held immediately to work in a. harmonious spirit seeking co-operative solutions to Canada's grave economic dilemma.

subsubtopic: USE OF FUNGICIDE CAPTAN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that Canadian health officials have known since 1978 of the health hazards, including cancer, miscarriages and birth defects, related to exposure to the fungicide Captan, and considering that Agriculture Canada has ignored the recommendation made by Health and Welfare Canada to ban or severely restrict the use of Captan, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House instruct the Department of Agriculture to issue immediately a strong warning to persons potentially at risk of exposure to Captan, and that this House immediately initiate a full parliamentary inquiry into the use of pesticides in Canada.

NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REGULATIONS GOVERNING AID PROJECTS-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On April 21 before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) stated that tied aid is a "minor league issue" and "a red herring", disregarding in the process mounds of evidence from independent researchers, the advice of Liberal foreign policy experts, Maurice Strong and Ivan Head, and the government's own 1975-1980 international development strategy. That this House direct the Government of Canada to adopt immediately the unanimous all-party recommendation of the parliamentary task force on North-South relations "that decisions concerning the procurement of goods and services required for aid projects should be made by the Canadian International Development Agency consistent with development assistance objectives. While a significant portion should be procured in Canada, CIDA should be freed from any fixed percentage rule".

subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMMEMORATIVE STAMP TO HONOUR ST. ALBERT, EDMONTON, ALTA.-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I seek the unanimous consent of the House to debate an urgent and important matter.
May 14, 1981

One hundred and twenty years ago one of the first missionaries of western Canada, Father Lacombe, founded the St. Albert mission in Alberta. That mission has contributed enormously to western Canada's growth over the years. Today St. Albert is a small city in the suburbs of Edmonton. The very identity of St. Albert is now being threatened by proposed annexation to the city of Edmonton. With a view to preserving a part of the historic character of St. Albert, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the government issue a commemorative stamp in honour of St. Albert and its founder, Father Lacombe, to highlight the one hundredth and twentieth anniversary of that town, and that the site where the mission was founded, which is now a provincial historic site, be declared a national monument.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. There are at least three federal judicial vacancies in the province of New Brunswick, with another to come up on July 1. One of these positions has been vacant since July 1, 1979. As a result there is a backlog of outstanding judgments of six months or more, and it is taking members of the legal profession over twice the amount of time it should to get files closed.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish):
That the House instruct the Minister of Justice to get on with the business of his portfolio and make these appointments so that the judicial system in New Brunswick can get back on the track.

IMPORTATION OF MEXICAN OIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. This Liberal government is buying Mexican oil in lumps and chunks at more than double the price of Alberta crude. After using a chain saw to get it out of the barrel-because Canadian drilling rigs are not available having left for the U.S.A.-and adding Alberta crude, eventually the mixture can be refined costing 150 per cent more than the cost of Alberta oil would have been now had the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) accepted the offer made by Premier Lougheed on July 25, 1980. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie):
That this House demands that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources responsible for this fiasco immediately resign, and the Canadian government wire Premier Lougheed that his offer of July 25, 1980, will now be accepted.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, who will know that he has achieved another record today. The Bank of Canada rate has been announced and it is up again slightly to a rate which has never before been exceeded in Canadian history. The minister knows, and has sometimes had the frankness to admit in this House, that one of the reasons for the high interest rate is the weakness of the Canadian dollar. He also knows that the single gravest threat to the strength of the Canadian dollar, coming from the policy of his government, is the National Energy Program.
In the interest of solving Canada's economic problems, will the Minister of Finance give us an undertaking now that there will be changes in the National Energy Program of a kind that will strengthen the Canadian dollar and begin to bring interest rates in this country back to a reasonable level?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CHANGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, without agreeing with all the comments in the preamble to the question, may I assure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition today, as I did yesterday in my statement in the House, that it is the intention of the Government of Canada to secure an agreement with the government of Alberta on the question of energy. Discussions to that effect are under way.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition specifically requests that changes be made. I believe my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has made it very clear that the Government of Canada is prepared to seek an accommodation, to be flexible; and that requires flexibility on the part of the government of Alberta. I believe, when I
expressed that sentiment, there was considerable agreement in the House yesterday that there is necessity to have an accommodation and a willingness to move on the part of the Government of Canada and on the part of the government of Alberta. That is what I would like to assure the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition about today.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: POSITION OF HOME OWNERS RENEWING MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one is tempted to ask the Minister of Finance how high he expects the Bank of Canada rate to be before his colleague is prepared to contemplate the kinds of changes which will result in an agreement. But let me come to another area of economic policy.
On Tuesday of this week in the House, the Minister of Finance indicated that he refused to help Canadian farmers and Canadian small businessmen who are now facing bankruptcy. The minister will know that there are some 500,000 Canadian home owners who are holding 1976 mortgages which are likely to come up for renewal this year. Does the Minister of Finance intend to introduce any specific help for these 500,000 Canadians who will be faced with staggering new costs when they renew their 1976 mortgages this year?

I would be pleased to repeat for the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition that it is not the intention of the government at the present time to bring in a special new program, which indeed would be very costly.
Yesterday the hon. member for St. John's West made a very vigorous exhortation to me to show expenditure restraint and to reduce the deficit. I believe in the long term that it is in the interests of all Canadians, including home owners and farmers, to take the steps now which will bring inflation down. I must say on this point that I tend to agree with the hon. member for St. John's West rather than the Leader of the Opposition.

This is the

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: CHAIRMANSHIP OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the only real growth in this government has been in interest rates, and they have gone up over 7 per cent since the budget came down.
My question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Finance could not tell us, or would not tell us, whether Mr. Maurice Strong, the ex-Liberal candidate, was being pushed by the government on the Canada Development Corporation. Today the Prime Minister announced that he would like to have Mr. Strong made head of the Canada Development Corporation. He also said that he would like to see the company play a more active role in federal industrial and economic plans, and provide a window on industry. Yesterday the Minister of Finance said there was no change in the role of the Canada Development Corporation. I can tell the Prime Minister this is a blow to investor confidence in Canada and the Canadian dollar will be under severe pressure after this further evidence of neglect of the private sector of this country.
Would the Prime Minister tell the House whether he intends to persist in forcing Mr. Strong upon the Canada Development Corporation, which is only 49 per cent government owned and 51 per cent owned by ordinary shareholders in this country- nearly 30,000 of them? Will the Prime Minister persist in this course and deal another blow to investor confidence in this country?

Madam Speaker, there is a small amount of confusion in the question asked by the hon. member. It is not a question of naming the president of the Canada Development Corporation. I think the Minister of Finance made it quite clear yesterday that he had confidence in the president of the CDC. It is a matter of the major shareholder, being the people of Canada represented by the Government of Canada through shares held by the Minister of Finance, wanting to have a say in the appointment of the chairman of the board. This does not seem like an extraordinary innovation. Our government and the preceding government had shown interest in naming chairmen of boards of Crown corporations in which it held all or part of the shares.

subtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE CHANGES IN POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there were two prospectuses which went out to the public of Canada, and a selling statement, in which the government made representations that the CDC would operate like a normal commercial corporation to maximize profits in the interests of all shareholders. Now the Prime Minister announces that he wants to change its role to a more active role in federal, that is, politically dictated, industrial and economic plans, and the other shareholders, the public shareholders, are forgotten.
My question to the Prime Minister is this: does Mr. Hamp-son, the president, agree with these efforts to push Mr. Strong on him? Does he agree with this new twisted role of this corporation, which is to be changed from its role that it had in these prospectuses? Does he agree with these matters?
My final question is this: is the Prime Minister prepared to buy out, at prices higher than the prices of several days ago when the shares started to drop in value as the result of reports of these interferences with the company by the government-is he prepared to buy out, at a considerable bonus, all of the innocent Canadian people who invested in this corporation on the government's fraudulent misrepresentations?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the reports in question are interesting and complete. They deserve serious consideration, a fact which I do not deny. However, the hon. member ought to keep in mind the fact that from now until the end of June we have hardly seven weeks left and that during those seven weeks the government must designate twelve opposition days, pursuant to the Standing Orders of the House. In fact we had one yesterday. That leaves eleven. Therefore at the rate of about two opposition days a week the government has barely two or three days left to put its bills through the House and complete this session with the best positive record possible for the well-being of the people of Canada.
In other words, I am saying to the hon. member that the reports in question are important. We do not deny that. But unfortunately the time left at our disposal in the House is too limited for us to devote one day or hours of debate to those reports which warrant debate and explanations and which indeed bear on the structure of the committees of the House. As it happens, I am now working on a draft document for submission to cabinet and I intend to hold consultations concerning a proposal for parliamentary reform in the not too distant future. It will be very difficult to concur in the recommendations of the reports referred to by the hon. member without first considering what we have in mind when it comes to reforming the committees of the House. Consequently we would be putting the cart before the horse if we were to accept those reports before reaching conclusions on the type of parliamentary reform we are prepared to study or consider.
Keeping those two factors in mind, lack of time and the link between the recommendations of those reports and the possibility of a parliamentary reform, I think that the most direct answer I can give the hon. member is that we will be unable to study those reports before the summer recess, but that should not be interpreted as lack of interest on our part. We will take them into account when the time comes to review the changes in the Standing Orders of the House.

No long-term government commitment can be made on the future of the Ottawa-Brock-ville service as a decision to continue or discontinue a service in the national railway passenger system is made based on a number of relevant economic and public interest factors e.g. current and projected operating costs and losses, the availability of alternate means of transportation, and the transportation needs of the communities served. speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
That this House deplores the record high interest rates imposed on Canadians by the Liberal government which together with double-digit inflation and slow economic growth are causing acute hardship and human suffering for Canadians, and demands that the government immediately introduce a budget and implement other economic programs to address these urgent and pressing problems.
He said: Mr. Speaker, for the past several months we in this Parliament have spent our time debating what amounted to the personal priority of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau).
In the motion we presented yesterday, and in the motion I am introducing today, we are saying that it is now time for the Parliament of Canada to give attention to the priorities of the people of this nation. Those priorities concern the resolution of our economic and energy problems, but particularly they are a means by which the Government of Canada can come to grips with inflation, unemployment and interest rates, problems which are causing very serious and real, human hardship to individual Canadians across the country.
We use question period and we use days like today, the only instruments available to an opposition, to raise issues. However, all that we can do in opposition is to raise these questions. The government alone has the power to resolve Canada's economic problems. By its actions the government has either made those problems worse, by driving jobs and investment out of Canada, or it has ignored the anger and the sense of betrayal which most Canadians feel about Ottawa's refusal to meet its responsibility of economic leadership.
What concerns Canadians are rising living costs that are making it impossible for the average wage earner to make ends meet; record interest rates that are forcing more and more small businesses and more and more Canadian farmers into bankruptcy; mortgage rates that turn the Canadian dream of owning a home into a financial nightmare; and a lack of economic growth and economic direction that has put a million Canadians out of work today and deeply threatens the job security of thousands more tomorrow.
The individual problems are acute enough, but this Liberal government's greatest crime against Canada now is that it is not even trying to face economic issues. The minister's policy is to do nothing. He says that anything he might do would only make matters worse.
Would it be worse for a pensioner to be getting an energy tax credit today? Would it be worse for a home buyer to be receiving a mortgage tax credit today? Would it be worse for a widow living in her own home to be receiving a property tax credit today? Of course it would not be worse. Those people need help and they need it now. The government's excuse that it cannot afford help for suffering Canadians is utterly false. It is an excuse that is denied by the government's own actions. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, I say to the House and I say to the government that if public money can buy an oil company like Petrofina, public money can protect Canadians against high energy costs and high accommodation costs.
Certainly the issue here is not the principle of spending. This government spends money like water. The question is the priority of spending. This Liberal government would sooner pay approximately a million dollars in a finder's fee to its millionaire friend, Maurice Strong, rather than pay $240 per family for an energy tax credit to low-income Canadians. That is not just raw patronage; that is contempt for Canadians in need.
May 14, 1981

speechtext: The minister of energy, who might want to put his seat on the line, says that is a lie. He is saying it is a lie that the Government of Canada paid $942,000 to the good Liberal friend, Maurice Strong.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
He can check the record, because in his own responses to the House he says it is a lie. His accusation is a matter which we will pursue in the House later on when he will be called upon to withdraw that allegation, defend it or surrender his seat.
In field after field the government is prepared to spend money on the wrong things but ignores the needs of ordinary Canadians who are caught in an economic squeeze. They increase by 17 per cent the amount of public money spent on consultants and on services, and they ignore Canadians who are caught with the prospect of bankruptcy or with high interest rates. They are buying Petrofina at a cost to the average Canadian energy user of $60 a year, yet they refuse to use that kind of tax money to help Canadians who are now facing serious economic problems.
They run a propaganda machine which has the government budget up now by $13.2 million from last year; it now stands at $62.8 million. They are prepared to help sell their own case to the people of Canada, but they are not prepared to make help available to individual Canadians in need. It is not a question of the principle of spending; it is a question of the priority of spending. The government put their own interests first and the interests of the people of Canada last. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we are all aware of the disastrous effects our present economic situation is having. The cost of living is increasing by over 12 per cent a year, which is the worst inflation rate we have had for over six years. The average Canadian who borrows is now paying the unprecedented interest rates of 20 per cent on a personal loan and 18 per cent on a mortgage loan. Commercial bankruptcies increased by 17 per cent last year and by over 20 per cent in the first quarter of this year. Farm bankruptcies are increasing at an even greater rate. Housing starts were low last year and will probably not increase much this year. One now needs a family income of $32,000 a year to get a mortgage on a standard house. Also, if we include those who are so discouraged that they do not even bother to register with the unemployment office, there are at least one million jobless in this country. What is even worse is that we are entering an age where technology threatens thousands of workers most of whom do not have the skills required to go from a job that automation made obsolete to another one which resulted from automation.
Bankruptcy for a small business, Mr. Speaker, is not merely a matter of statistics, it affects men and women who devoted
The Economy
their lives and invested their money to build something and who suddenly see their hopes shattered. When a farmer must give up his land because he can no longer meet his bank payments, not only does this constitute a crime against a world hungry for all that we can produce, but it is also a case where a family becomes uprooted and where often a way of life, handed down from generation to generation, based on the love of the land ceases to exist.

When a young couple finds that saving every available cent will not get them a home, or where renewing a mortgage means finding $300 more per month that one does not have, it is not just an economic problem. It means that families who came to this country believing that Canada was a place in which they could get ahead if they were prepared to work begin to question the promise of Canada. If you are a telephone operator, an insurance clerk, an auto worker, or a worker in any other industry where technology and machines are replacing people, you cannot avoid asking yourself if your job is next and, even more troubling, what you will do with work skills society does not seem to need any more. Those are the real economic issues of Canada because they are the issues which directly touch the lives of Canadians. Of course the problems are complex. Governments are elected to resolve complex problems. The minister says, "It is so difficult I will not do anything". If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) were Noah, he would say, "I will not build an ark because it is raining too hard".
The minister is protected against the consequences of his do-nothing policy. He is protected by his comfortable minister's salary and by the complacency of being too long in office. The people he was elected to care about are not protected, and the people he used to pretend to care about are not protected.
The government came into office by being against an 18-cent per gallon increase in the cost of gasoline and they have since raised the price 52 cents per gallon. Now the minister says that Canadians should absorb that increase and pay for it out of money he claims they have. Where does the minister think all this loose money is in the budget of the average Canadian family? It is not in their housing budgets with mortgage rates at 18 per cent. It is not in their food budgets with food costs up 15 per cent from a year ago. It will not come out of rising incomes because the government's own statistics show that incomes have been declining in real terms for the last few years.
The only economic policy to come from this government has been to hurt people who need help. The government's major economic initiative has been the national energy policy, which is driving Canadian jobs and Canadian investment out of Canada. Instead of building on energy, the Liberal government is crippling what could be the single strongest growth factor in our economy.
Its other initiative is to blame it all on Bouey, to pretend that the government is not responsible for economic policy, it is just the Bank of Canada. If the minister were more honest, he would admit that he is only taking half the advice of the

May 14, 1981
The Economy
Bank of Canada. He accepts that part of the bank's advice which is hard on people, but he ignores that part of the bank's advice which requires sacrifice by his own government. Governor Bouey has often made it clear that it is very difficult for him to dampen credit demand if the country's largest creditor, the federal government, continues to make massive borrowings to finance its deficits. That is exactly what the minister is doing. Canada's economic situation is the following: we have no Minister of Finance and we have only half of Gerald Bouey. [Translation]
The minister-who, incidentally, has become the invisible man-is faced with two very simple alternatives. He can live up to the economic challenge and start to show the leadership that the nation expects of him, or else he can resign as we asked yesterday. If he stays on as a minister, he must without delay introduce a budget, not in the fall, but before the end of this session. He has held his portfolio for nearly 15 months and he has not yet clearly explained his economic policy to the country.
It is essential that we have a budget, and in this budget the minister must deal with two basic issues. First, he must attack squarely the issue of inflation, especially as concerns the current interest rates, which have reached a record high. If the minister believes that his monetary policy is inadequate, time has come to change it. I say his policy because there is no doubt that, in his capacity as Minister of Finance, he has the last word and the ultimate responsibility regarding monetary issues such as interest rates. He cannot hide behind the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
On the other hand, if the minister believes that his present policy of high interest rates remains the most appropriate for Canada, he must act accordingly and heed the advice of the Bank of Canada, which is to reduce the federal deficit. If he wants to maintain his policy of high interest rates, his budget must provide assistance for the Canadians who are the hardest hit by a double-digit inflation. The minister says that he does not have much room to manoeuvre. We faced the same dilemma when we came to power and inherited the financial mess created by hon. members opposite during the last decade. But we took our responsibilities; we made the hard decisions which were required; the Crosbie budget contained proposals designed to help low and medium income Canadians.
This must become a priority in the Minister's budget. It is about time for him and the government to start saying to Canadians how they expect our economy to develop in the coming decade, and especially how they expect to provide employment opportunities and employment security for Canadians in the eighties.
Mr. Speaker, three great tasks await us if we want to give to Canadians the kind of economic future that this country is capable of. First, we have to produce enough jobs, at least 1.5
million new jobs over the next four years, if we are to make a reasonable dent in the rate of unemployment, if we are to absorb new entrants into the labour force and if we are to provide alternate employment to women and others who are displaced by advanced technology.
Second, we must create the right kind of jobs. We do not need make-work programs which offer marginal pay today and no future tomorrow. We need jobs in the growth industries of the future, the kind of rewarding jobs which excite people and which they know will exist and grow in the years to come. In this country we have the potential to create those kinds of jobs. We have industries, electronics, transportation, northern development, oceanography, as well as energy and food. These are the kinds of industries where we can be among the leaders of the world if we have strong national leadership and effective programs to support our own companies. It is time we began receiving that leadership from this government and seeing those programs emanating from it.
Finally, we must ensure that Canadians who need jobs have the skills and training necessary to qualify for the opportunities we create. We are facing a mammoth problem in that regard. Among our current unemployed we have literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians who simply lack the skills needed to qualify for anything but the most marginal and menial kinds of jobs. The problem will get worse. A recent conference reported that as many as one million women could lose their current jobs during the 1980s to advanced technology. There are estimates that in the auto industry alone as many as 20 per cent of the existing jobs could be lost to automation.
We are dealing with an economic crisis today which was created over the last ten years. This government can do much more for Canadians in need. Its flexibility is limited by the deficits of John Turner, Donald Macdonald and past Fiberal ministers. But just as the lack of economic courage in the past created problems today, the lack of economic courage today will create problems for the future of Canada. The nature of jobs in Canada is changing. Many traditional jobs will no longer exist. Many people now working will see their jobs lost to technology. Much of the training available to Canadians today is looking backward rather than forward. We have to build job security for the future. That must start now, and it can only start with federal leadership.
[ Translation]
When we were in power, we made plans for a conference on economic development in Winnipeg to be held in February of last year. I therefore find it most regrettable that this government should not have shown any real interest in pursuing the matter any further. I deplore the arrogant way in which the Prime Minister has turned down the constructive proposal made by the Premier of Ontario that the first ministers meet to discuss the economic challenges of the nation. A responsible national government would not have missed such a great opportunity of finding a solution in consultation with the provinces.
May 14, 1981

The new budget must come to grips with today's urgent problems, but it must also, and without delay, provide measures capable of guaranteeing Canadians security of employment in the years to come. If nothing is done now, not only will all Canadians suffer but there may also be two specific categories of victims: young people and women. Our young people need new training to be able to tackle the jobs of tomorrow. Women who want to join the labour market or acquire new skills are in need of better opportunities, better orientation and better incentives. We must give priority to jobs which will make it possible for our women, our young people and other Canadians to contemplate with confidence a secure future on the labour market.
We have here, in Canada, the energy, the food and the other resources we need to develop fully. We also have an industrial base which can cope more and more with international competition. Our labour force is young, well trained and dedicated. In spite of their current preoccupations, the uncertainty and the apprehension which they must face today, Canadians still have faith in their country. What they need is leadership and this they expect from their national leaders. They can meet the challenges today if they are assured of a better future. [English]
The government has been ignoring its economic responsibility. It has been driving Canadians into bankruptcy, despair and anger. It has been abandoning its responsibilities to help Canadians prepare for a future which will be profoundly changed but which can be profoundly promising for this country if we have the wisdom and the courage to seize that future. We have been following the Prime Minister's personal priorities for six months now in the House of Commons. It is time to give the priorities of the people of Canada a chance.

It is time for this government to put aside its preoccupation and to realize that there is a country which wants to build, that there are people who want to be free of the burdens of economic policy placed upon them by this government and that there are individuals who are prepared to go out and work to build a secure future for the country. This must be recognized by the government. The place to start is with a new budget-soon, before the end of June. We must not wait again, ducking behind other elements of policy as was done the last time. We need a new national budget but, most important, we need a new commitment by this government, a commitment which recognizes that the people of Canada have priorities too and that those are priorities which have been ignored. These priorities can no longer be ignored.
Our country was built upon respect for individuals who were prepared to go forward and make a mark for themselves. This government is making that more difficult every day. We live in a country which can become one of the strongest nations in the world if we are prepared to use our resources and take account of the changing world of work. This government must give some kind of leadership. That can come only if there is a

willingness on the part of the government to put its personal priorities behind and to adopt and confront the priorities of the people of Canada. That is what this motion urges the government to do. We devoutly hope that it will act on that, that it will bring in a budget, that it will begin to pay attention to the problems and to the immense potential of the people of this country.

speechtext:
However, it reflects the attitude of the government. I do not object to the concerns which the government has had with the Constitution as that is, indeed, an important matter. However, we in this House all know the Prime Minister has shown no interest or concern with the question of economics since he became Prime Minister of this country. That is demonstrated by his response today, and more particularly by the government's over-all response by having neither himself nor the Minister of Finance enter into this important debate.
I now want to turn to the specific subject matter. At the root of the government's lack of policy is its commitment to the perpetuation of a myth which has been established, at this point in the twentieth century, not only in Canada with the present government but also in the United States of America and in Great Britain; that is the myth that in dealing with inflation a government should adopt a policy that forces up the cost of everything we buy and almost everything we consume.
In short, the high interest rate policy which is being pursued by this government is exactly the same in its effects on people as would be an admonition to a drowning man that he would be saved if we only made the water just a bit deeper. That is the kind of economic brilliance this government is displaying in the pursuit of its high interest rate policy.
The experience of Margaret Thatcher in the United Kingdom, or that of President Carter and his successor, President Reagan, in the United States, and the previous experience of Liberal administrations and that of the Leader of the Opposition, ought to have shown this government that rather than curbing inflation or reducing the cost of living, a high interest rate policy does just the opposite.
I want to come back and deal with some proposals. The kinds of suggestions we are making, contrary to what the Minister of Finance has said in his blanket condemnation about opposition suggestions being inflationary, would have quite the opposite effect. 1 hope he changes his mind and participates in this debate soon.
Now that we are in a situation where workers are in their fourth year in a row with a decline in the standard of living, when we are now at almost 12.5 per cent inflation, when just this afternoon we heard that we have set a record in Canadian history for interest rates, I would like to ask, when is it going to end?
The general situation has not been described better than in words which were uttered not long ago in the House of Commons, and I would like to quote them as they relate to the effects of this kind of high interest rate policy, because I think that that is the core of the current problem. It is by no means the whole problem, as I will indicate later. This is what was said just a while ago in the House of Commons:
The present record level of interest rates,.... cuts back the ability of Canadians to buy goods and services of all kinds-cars, homes, food and clothing, everything people need. These high interest rates cut back the ability of factories and businesses generally to expand, to create more production and jobs. These high interest rates limit the ability of business, especially small business, simply to operate at basic non-inflationary levels. Therefore these high interest rates mean losses of production and jobs now and over the coming winter months.
The Conservative government has been saying that these high interest rates are needed to fight inflation, but they in themselves drive up costs and add to inflation. All this has been demonstrated by the jump in the cost of living-
Then of one full point.
-obviously incorporating increases in costs due to increases in interest rates. The government has allowed these increases to go into effect in the period since it has been in office.
These words which, as I say, are quite accurate as a general description of the high interest rate policy and its impact on our kind of economy, were uttered by the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) when he was finance critic for the Liberal party when they were in opposition. The point is that what the minister said when he was in opposition is just as true today as it was in 1979, and just as the high interest rate policy did more harm than good then, it does so now. Just as it was an inappropriate policy when it was pursued by the Conservatives, so, too, is it an inappropriate policy which is being pursued by the Liberals.

I want to ask: When is the message finally going to get home to the government? When is it going to abandon an intellectual commitment to an ossified theory- this absurd preoccupation with monetarism which is now as deeply embedded in the Government of Canada as it is in the government of the United Kingdom and in the government of the United States?
Are we going to wait until the number of families which have to abandon their homes reaches 1,100 a month instead of 1,000? Are we going to wait until a record number of small businessmen have to organize and come to demonstrate on Parliament Hill? Are we going to wait until thousands of additional farmers have to abandon their herds because they cannot meet the interest rate level needed to maintain their existence? Workers have become exasperated with the fact that their living standards have declined three years in a row, so that on the average they have lost $35 a week in real disposable income. Will this loss have to increase to $40 or $50 a week before they must literally organize some riots to force the government to act?
Will the poor finally organize? We just learned, in what I consider to be a very moving and deeply disturbing report not many days ago, that the people who are disproportionately affected by high interest rate charges are the poor. As the people responsible for the study indicated, the poor are more deeply in debt, not because they are buying coloured television sets or taking holidays in Florida or anywhere else, but because they are buying the necessities of life. Are the poor finally going to have to get exasperated, come to Ottawa and force this government to act?
The point is that this MacEachen monetary madness must stop; the people of Canada will have to rise up and force the government to abandon this policy.

Hear, hear!
May 14, 1981

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
The motion before the House calls for a new budget, and we agree. The other day and also in the past our financial critic, on behalf of our party, outlined a number of measures which would be appropriate in a new budget, not simply to deal with the question of inflation, but to deal with the long-range structural problem of the Canadian economy which must be dealt with if we are to have full employment.
Today I want to deal with those measures, specifically in the context of dealing with the question of inflation in a serious way. I hope the government will have the honesty today to do what it did not do yesterday in the debate: that is, to reply to the points which are made; not to sit there in arrogant indifference while listening to what is being said on this side of the House, but to take on the arguments. If our arguments are shown to be wrong, we will admit they are wrong. However, we want this serious matter dealt with in a serious way.
Before going to three of four very specific suggestions on how to deal with inflation, I must say that although I have indicated my party agrees with some of the suggestions which the official opposition has made in terms of dealing with inflation, there is one matter on which we frankly cannot accept any criticism from their corner, and that is the interest rate policy itself.
The Leader of the Opposition should know better than anyone else in the House of Commons, perhaps, in spite of his own criticism as Leader of the Opposition before he became prime minister, that when he was in office interest rates not only went up one, two or three times, but more than that. So when it comes to interest rate policy, neither we nor anyone else has to listen to the Conservative Party of Canada. However, I want to put that aside. The Liberal party is the government of the day and it has the responsibility to deal with the important matter before us.
I now want to suggest three or four specific ways of dealing particularly with the pervasive problem of inflation. In so doing, I repeat that I want to see the government put up or shut up today and to respond to the arguments. More than respond to the arguments, I would like to see the government act on them if it agrees with them.
First is the question of interest rates. I have already said that the evidence is overwhelmingly clear to everyone, except someone who gets so rigidly locked into some economic theory that he decides to lock out all the evidence, that the increase in interest rates has not resulted at all in a reduction of the cost of living but has had the opposite effect.
What do we say should be done? We are saying that instead of sitting back and responding in a knee-jerk reaction to what takes place in the United States in terms of interest rates, we should move in the opposite direction. At his regular meetings with the Governor of the Bank of Canada, or by telephone, the Minister of Finance should make it clear that he expects the Bank of Canada to start moving immediately, step by step, in the direction of a reduced interest rate policy in order to bring
The Economy
interest rates down to roughly the level of inflation in Canada. We think that would work.
I want to say to the Minister of Finance that if there is a run on the dollar or if there is a concern about a flow of money south of the border in the short run, then certain action could be taken. We do not withdraw from the suggestion of a form of exchange controls. The minister should know better than anyone else that some form of exchange controls has been put in place by many countries in western Europe and by the United States. In fact, the administration of John F. Kennedy in 1963 and that of Richard Nixon in the early 1970s introduced special measures to deal with the problem of the outflow of capital. They showed a little more imagination than has been demonstrated by the Government of Canada. When President Kennedy was in office he introduced for a limited period of time a special tax intended to discourage the outflow of capital. That practice was duplicated almost a decade later by President Nixon.
I say to the Minister of Finance that it is hardly a radical idea and hardly a profound change. Some countries in Europe and also the United States have done this. I repeat, this party does not back away from a little innovation. If we need a limited form of control to deal with a possible export of capital, then the New Democratic Party says, "Let's do it if it benefits the people of Canada".

speechtext:
A second area in which the government could act is in the domain of energy prices, on certain aspects of prices. It could consider seriously the government study done over many years which showed that the oil companies had been ripping off consumers from 1958 to 1973 to the tune of $500 for every man, woman and child in Canada. We all know that this has gone on to an equal or greater degree since.
What is an appropriate response to this? I see the Minister of Finance has been joined by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) who obstensibly is going to reply. They are sitting there giggling over the situation. 1 should like them to consider the argument again. The argument is that if there is a report which shows that the oil companies have gouged the people of Canada by $500 per citizen over that period of time and which makes recommendations on how to lower energy costs, why would the Liberal government not act if it is concerned about the impact of energy prices on the people of Canada?
In our view, the following suggestions are workable. First of all, by a price reduction of a few cents per gallon the government could order a reduction at the retail outlet level in the price of petroleum to compensate the Canadian consumer for that great loss. I speak not only of the consumer buying gasoline for his or her car but also of the consumer buying fuel to heat his home. A price reduction which was aimed at getting back for the consumer that money which has been gouged from him would make sense and would reduce the cost of living.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
As the study pointed out, one of the major reasons for the excess profits or charges was the multinational structure which enabled Exxon Corporation to overcharge Imperial Oil which, as the price leader in the market in Canada, in turn passed on excess prices to the people of Canada. There is a solution to that problem as well, and that is to do what other countries have done with state-owned oil companies, and that is in our case to make Petro-Canada the exclusive importer. Prices passed on to all retail outlets in Canada could be passed on at a reduced level. I repeat, that is a practical suggestion that would not be inflationary.
Let me deal with one other aspect of energy costs. We now subsidize the price of energy in Atlantic Canada but we do nothing for people who live in our northern regions. People have to pay higher prices in all northern communities across Canada. We recommend that there should be a slight fuel subsidy for northern Canadians in order to bring the price of gasoline and home heating fuel in northern communities across the land down to the average national level. So much for energy prices, Mr. Speaker. I repeat, I do not think that suggestion is inflationary at all; it is non-inflationary and would help reduce the cost of living.
Now I come to high prices. We have said that the government has constitutional authority to act now to establish a fair prices commission to administer key prices in the economy. This is not a revolutionary idea. The Prime Minister misled the House a while ago when he said that the government did not have that authority. That is absurd. It has the same constitutional authority to do in practice what it did when it brought in a wage control program a few years ago. This time we say that it should do something to act on behalf of workers instead of against them.
A fair prices commission would act in a flexible way. It could force reductions where price increases occurred that were unjustified in terms of reasonable profit margins. It would not take action, obviously, against all price increases. Again, this is not an inflationary kind of government response.
My next proposal is a tax reduction to assist average and low-income people. As I suggested in two election campaigns, and as our finance critic mentioned yesterday in the House and before that in previous debates, if this were complemented with serious tax reform that would deal with the banks' excess profits, tax loopholes for the corporate sector and for private individuals, there could be this kind of tax reduction which would help poor people cope with inflation without increasing the debt of Canada at all.
Another item is housing. Of all the countries in the world that ought to have established adequate housing as a right for its people, surely Canada ought to have been doing that a long time ago. Instead of seeing 1,000 families per month having to abandon their houses, we should be seeing 1,000 families moving into new housing. It is only because of the government's inaction in this regard that we do not see housing established as a universal right, like medicare, in Canada.
What would we do? Instead of CMHC buying up houses that people have had to abandon and then selling them at a
loss, we would at least take steps to extend mortgages to enable people to maintain their homes instead of abandoning them. Beyond that, we would say that in a country that produces lumber in the way we do and which still has more than one million workers unemployed, instead of failing to spend the CMHC budget on non-profit and co-op housing, we should deal with the needs of renters in Canada and the needs of people who desire co-op housing by significantly expanding these budgets to ensure that housing is available. That would deal with job creation, and in the not so long run would increase the supply of housing and have the effect of driving down the price of housing as well.
There is something which characterizes these few points I have made. First, in our view they are not inflationary. Second, they would have the effect of reducing costs in a serious, tangible way for ordinary Canadians. Third-and this is the reason I suggest we get no action from the government, from the Liberals and as well from the Conservatives-the kinds of proposals I have advocated here are objectionable not because they are inflationary but because they require, on the one hand, taking action against the banks or oil companies in a tough-minded way, which those two parties do not like to do, or they would require a more activist government in the economy. That really gets at the nub of it.
Whether we talk about a fair prices commission, expansion in the housing sector or the government's having a deepening role in the energy sector, all of these points mean the kind of thing that Francois Mitterand represents in France today, that Helmut Schmidt represents in Germany today, and Olaf Palme will represent when he is returned as prime minister of Sweden in an election that will probably take place next month. They reflect a social democratic philosophy which says that government activity of itself is not evil. I say to the Minister of Finance that it was government activity which moved this country into medicare, took it out of the market system, and did the same earlier with pensions. We are saying in these sectors of the economy that we need a little more government involvement. That is not bad.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are getting to your feet. I will conclude in one minute. Just as the people of Canada accepted government involvement in pensions and the government establishment of medicare, so too in dealing with a crisis economy the people of Canada would accept the kind of innovative government action I am advocating here today.
If I have the patience of the House, and I see you are getting to your feet, Mr. Speaker, I will conclude with one observation.

I want to conclude with the following observation. When the Conservatives were in power for a brief period of time, the Liberals had a saying about the Conservatives. They said the people of Canada had a non-government. With the deception that has been inflicted upon the people of Canada by the Liberals since they have come back to office, with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), to name two, promising certain things to the people of Canada and their systematically being denied implementation by the Minister of Finance, we have replaced a "non-government" with what can only be described as a "con government". speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I feel badly that the Leader of the New Democratic Party has a sense of outrage that his fresh participation is not being responded to by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I remind him that the Minister of Finance has now spent a full two days in this House dealing with the debate. We are very pleased to welcome the Leader of the New Democratic Party and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) to this debate for the first time. We are very pleased to have them here. It is nice to have them drop in on us like this. It is nice to have them show that for 30 minutes or so they are able to take some time out of their travelling arrangements to drop into the House of Commons to discuss this very important topic.
We certainly share many of the concerns that are being raised in the economic questions that are being posed in this debate. The Leader of the Opposition is a little wrong, as he often is, in describing this as the first time this government has come to grips with the economic issue. If he had spent more time in the House or spent a little more time calculating what went on, he would realize that we have spent more time in this session of Parliament debating economic matters than we have matters concerning the Constitution. His own obsession and preoccupation with his losing cause in the Constitution is no reason to judge other people by what he sees in his own reflection. The fact is we have spent a good deal of time and have taken a number of significant and important initiatives in coming to grips with the economic conditions being faced in Canada.
Unlike members opposite, we do not pretend we have the magic solution, the simple panaceas. That is one of the luxuries that can be afforded by the perpetual state of opposition in which hon. ladies and gentlemen opposite find themselves. They do not have to deal with the responsibility of making tough choices and coming to grips with the realities. They can concoct their own realities and develop their own mythology.
The Economy
They have become the great myth machine in Canada in trying to describe an economic landscape which simply is not there.
This is why it is important that we have the opportunity to try to clarify what kinds of real conditions do exist and the kinds of initiatives that we in this country are putting forward as ways of responding to them. These are real issues and real solutions, not the fantasy-like island which the Leader of the Opposition has been on for so long. It is not the kind of ideological rigidity of the framework in which the Leader of the New Democratic Party exists, with answers or solutions simply being drawn from age old, traditional orthodoxies upon which they solely exist because any sense of innovation is totally lacking.
I remind the Leader of the Opposition that one mythology he would be very wise to overcome is the feeling on his part that he was defeated a year and a half ago. He was not defeated, he defeated himself.
One of the ironies is that we have a group opposite talking to us about how we should be more realistic in looking at economic figures. They could not even add up the number of members they had in the House of Commons on December 13, a year and a half ago. If they cannot add up to 282, I suggest it places in some doubt their ability to deal with numbers that are a little more complicated and perhaps more complex.
We in Canada have to face the fact that the economic landscape is changing. The terrain we have to traverse is not as it was ten years ago, or even two or three years ago. There are a number of significant economic changes taking place. No one has a clear road map as to what the precise direction must be.
Every country in the industrialized world, in fact every country around the world, is searching for those kinds of solutions. I would hope that we would use this debate for a mutual search for solutions, not for acrimony, not for the kind of adversarial nonsense that we hear, but for a genuine attempt to find what kind of leadership can be given, not just from the government sector but from the private sector as well. Because this is a responsibility shared by all sectors of the economy. This is not something which we can provide for the villains of the piece. It does not fit some morality play. It will require the full involvement and contribution of businessmen, labour people, and government officials at all levels to come to grips with these kinds of questions. That is what we are trying to do, to develop a series of signals that will provide the kind of direction which other major actors and players in this economy can follow.
The first thing we have to understand is that there are parts of the economy that we must assess as being at the present time positive, useful and constructive. The Leader of the Opposition is still reading old speeches. He has not quite been able to update his material yet. He is like an old actor who simply repeats the same old lines.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
The fact of the matter is that when he concentrates on matters of employment creation in this country there is no doubt, by every indicator that is available, that the economic performance of this country far surpasses that of any other country in the industrial world. We have created 346,000 jobs in one year. To try to pretend that somehow that fact does not exist, that it is not a fact of life, simply means that the Leader of the Opposition has either forgotten to read or refuses to face reality. In fact, they do the economy of this country a disservice by constantly conjuring up these images of 1.5 million unemployed. The figures speak for themselves. They are there in black and white. The unemployment rate is down to 7 per cent, the best record since 1976. The growth rate of employment is 3.3 per cent, which far surpasses that of the United States, West Germany and Great Britain.
Let us talk for a minute about Great Britain, I have heard members opposite talk with a great deal of pride and admiration about the remarkable economic theories of their counterparts in Great Britain. We have heard the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) talk with great enthusiasm about the magic solutions of Margaret Thatcher. I will tell the House what those magic solutions have created. They have created an unemployment rate of 11 per cent in Great Britain, a full four points higher than we have in this country. If we followed the sort of musings of the Conservative party, the kind of admonition they have raised that we should follow the example of Great Britain, then we would have several hundreds of thousands of additional Canadians out of work. In fact, if we followed the admonitions that were put forward in the Crosbie budget, we would have more Canadians out of work than there are right now.
We were not prepared to adopt the savage-like cuts that would have created an enormous sort of recessionary impulse in this country and put Canadians out of work. We were not prepared to follow the kind of exorbitant and extravagant oil prices which again would have thrown the economy out of kilter and created unemployment for Canadians. The fact of the matter is that we all have to face the reality of rising oil prices, but to bring them in in the kind of cold turkey fashion the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) prophesied a year and a half ago would have given enormous jolts to the economy of this country, something we were not prepared to accept, which in turn led the Canadian people, in their judgment, to adopt our proposals.
If we look at oil pricing-and this really is one of the major inflationary pushes-we realize that if you increase the price of oil by 100 per cent, that will add almost a full 10 percentage points to the inflation rate. What would have happened if we had followed the Conservative oil pricing policy is that we would have had substantially higher oil prices. In our estimation we would have had an additional 100,000 people out of work.

I do not know if the Leader of the Opposition is really serious, but if he looked at the Gallup poll that showed 80 per cent of Canadians felt that the proposals in our constitutional position were adding to the unity of this country, he might do some rethinking about his own absurd positions which he has adopted in this House over the past six months.
I would also like to say to him, Mr. Speaker, this great defender of transferring resources to provincial governments, combined with the kind of position taken by his colleagues in saying that it is this government that is responsible, that he should take one look, if he can spend his time away from his defence of his position amongst his colleagues, at the real facts and figures. He might then realize that over the last year the big spenders in this country, the people who added to the growth of government, were not those at the federal level. We had a 1.5 per cent growth rate of public employees. It was those provincial governments which he defends that added 14
May 14, 1981

per cent to the growth of public employees in Canada. When this government asks for more authority to manage the national economy, it is because we need to provide for a greater degree of control and management of a national scheme so as not to allow that fragmentation, of which he is an advocate, which would permit the economy to get out of shape and out of whack.
I think it is worth talking about some of the positions put forward by the NDP in this area. They talk about their solutions to the problems. Perhaps one of the most inflationary positions we face is that their supply of solutions far exceeds the demand. They are simply out of date on this. They say they are prepared to accept foreign exchange controls. Let us just ask what the result of that might be for a moment. Let us put the case to Canadians as to what the result of a falling dollar and foreign exchange controls might be.
First, there is the whole question of policing. Perhaps the experience the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) might want to examine is that of other countries who have foreign exchange controls and the wide variety of schemes and gimmicks that are used to get around those controls. The fact of the matter is that the primary beneficiaries of foreign exchange controls are the large financial institutions which he does not like. It is the Canadian consumer, the small person, who suffers under exchange controls, because he is the one who does not have the sophistication to find the tools with which they can slice their money.
I think it would be useful for the Leader of the New Democratic Party to examine that particular proposal he is making. I am afraid he would end up hurting the very people he wants to help, and he would hurt them even more by a falling dollar. Because the immediate result of that would not be to cut into the economic growth of this country, because we are already at virtually full capacity; what would happen-

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that if the Leader of the NDP paid less attention to the response of other people and paid a little more attention to the comments
The Economy
we are making, he would realize that we have had in the past year an employment growth rate of 3.3 per cent, amounting to the creation of 346,000 additional jobs, which far exceeds the record of any other economy in the western world.
If he looks at manufacturing, mining and industrial processing, he will find that we are virtually bumping up against our capacity to produce. One of the real discussions we should be having in this House is with respect to the issue of how to deal with the bottlenecks in our economy. How can we come to grips with the shortages of skilled workers which are developing? How do we deal with capital supply? Again what the Leader of the New Democratic Party forgets, with his peculiar economic theory, is that foreign exchange controls would have a very severe repercussion on the capital flows into this country which are required for investment in new mines, new machinery, new factories and new plants. In other words, his particular nostrum or panacea is restricting growth, imposing higher costs on consumers and developing another way of providing advantages to the very wealthy financial institutions in this country which can move their money around at ease. The small, average Canadian cannot do that. That would be the result of the policies put forward by the Leader of the New Democratic Party.
I think it useful in this economic debate that we talk about some of the proposals we have put forward. I think the Leader of the Opposition referred to the areas of employment and training as being areas where leadership is required. I suggest that that is exactly what we have been providing. While the Leader of the Opposition has been involved in the protection and defence of his own political position, he somehow has not been recognizing what has been put forward as a series of initiatives to deal with employment and training in order to provide workers with greater skills and provide greater opportunities for women and native people to obtain the skills they need.
I would like to take a minute, if I might, to talk about leadership in coming to grips with the structural problems of the labour market and responding to the need for new training. We have just finished signing a series of agreements with major industrial groups in Canada regarding aerospace, shipbuilding, mining, coal mining and construction so as to develop planning arrangements, human resource planning and skill training arrangements to enable us to work in total co-operation and in conjunction with major industrial sectors. This will enable us to have a clear assessment of their human resource needs, so that we can apply new training programs to their needs and introduce affirmative action programs to ensure equality of opportunity for those who have been excluded from the labour force.
We signed one agreement yesterday with the aerospace industry. Tomorrow I will be signing one with the shipbuilding industry. We are making those kinds of agreements in order to come to grips with the very problems identified by the Leader of the Opposition.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
We have introduced a new training program for women in non-traditional work. That program has been greeted with a great deal of support. It is now providing the opportunity for women to move into fields such as pipefitting, machinery and welding. These are areas from which women have long been excluded. That is a program that is now being adopted across this country.
We have just introduced a new program to help the physically handicapped obtain their first jobs. That is a $52 million program which the Leader of the Opposition has not come across.
We introduced in the budget of the Minister of Finance the industrial adjustment program, which is an innovative way of dealing with the problems of industrial change and industrial obsolescence. We will now provide direct assistance to workers who are displaced from their jobs because the factories at which they were employed no longer produce products which are needed. That program is now available in five communities and will be available in others. That is one way by which we work together with local businessmen, labour people and provincial government officials to come to grips with the problems of industrial change and adjustment. That again is an example of how we are trying to take a comprehensive and cohesive approach to developing better skills in this country.
We have introduced employment programs which have shifted the resources of this government to help those who have the greatest difficulty in the workplace. We have introduced for the first time an affirmative action program in our own public service to provide leadership in the hiring of women, disabled people and native people in this country. We have worked out a number of new agreements respecting large megaprojects so that they will provide greater assistance to natives to find employment and training opportunities. At the same time we have provided an additional native training assistance program.
For one year I think that is not a bad record. It begins to show that we have put into place a number of new programs. We believe those programs in themselves are not enough, and we must take a still much broader approach to the problem. That is one reason this government recommended the establishment of a parliamentary task force, which will be reporting in a month or so. The task force has spent a full six or seven months crossing Canada, consulting Canadians and coming up with solutions to the very employment and training programs the Leader of the Opposition was so concerned about.
My own department has been working and developing new data analyses and will be coming forward with a statement in a matter of three or four weeks putting forward a number of recommendations which we hope to use in consultation with the provinces and the private sector to provide for a full range of new solutions to the labour market problems of the 1980s.
We believe that one of the most effective ways of dealing with inflation in this country is to tackle the bottlenecks in the economy, to look at where shortages exist and to develop responses which are effective and useful. However, we recognize that solutions cannot be adopted unilaterally. We cannot
conjure up solutions from a magician's hat. We cannot pull answers out of some old Fabian pamphlet the Leader of the New Democratic Party carries around. The answers must be based on up-to-date analyses and arrived at in full consultation with all the partners in the economy. They must be worked out in conjunction with those partners. We must obtain the cooperation of the trade unions with respect to changing practices and providing for greater mobility of workers in Canada so that they will go where the jobs are. We must work out, in co-operation with the industrial companies of this country, new training programs which provide, for the first time, a much higher degree of support in relation to the introduction of on-site industrial training programs. We must work out with the provinces an understanding of how we must change our training allocations, which are decided by provincial governments' in order to develop more up-to-date and relevant training opportunities for Canadians.
I suggest to this House and to Canadians that we are trying to provide real leadership in coming to grips with the structural problems of labour in this country and in providing the initiatives and innovations which will signal to other major actors in the Canadian economy solutions and answers to those kinds of problems. This indicates that we work in partnership and consultation and that we are prepared to work with all sectors of the Canadian economy in finding the solutions which are needed.
We are not here to pretend that somehow the economy of Canada can be changed overnight. It is a very painstaking and at times very difficult process to bring about real reform and change.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that in the first year we have put the building blocks in place. We have initiated programs. We have initiated the analyses and the consultations which are required. At the same time, I think it is true to our principles and philosophy that we have been prepared to accept and introduce those programs which would provide a cushion and a support for those in the economy who are hurt by inflation and who are sometimes the losers when other incomes go up. I remind hon. members that ours is one of the few countries in the industrial world which has an indexing of the income tax system. That program costs the treasury substantial amounts of money. It is very easy to point to the United States as an example, but the United States does not have the income tax index we do in this country. That provides a major degree of support for those Canadian consumers about whom we have heard so much. It provides us with the ability to keep taxes in line with incomes on an inflationary basis. I suggest that that is a very important support for the Canadian consumer.
We have also introduced supports in the area of helping older people through income supplement programs. That is a very necessary support for those who do not have incomes which rise as fast as the incomes of those who have unions
May 14, 1981

working for them or those who are organized and have full wage opportunities.
We have provided for a degree of support in other areas in the economy. Individuals are being cushioned. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation provides a non-profit housing program which is prepared to provide rental housing at interest rates of no more than 1 per cent or 2 per cent at the present moment. If hon. members do not think the minister responsible for housing is not crying about the fact that he cannot do more, he is, but that is a program which is one of the major suppliers of rental housing across Canada. The federal government is putting up capital to supply housing, whereas many of our provincial counterparts simply will not introduce comparable housing programs.
At the same time the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has introduced programs to deal with price-fixing. He has examined the oil industry. He is providing answers. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Roberts) has introduced major programs to increase research spending in this country up to 22 per cent. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has been able to obtain major advantages for medical research in this country. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has provided for additional funding through DIP and other means in order to increase productivity.
Over the past year we have been trying to redress some of the serious and grievous errors made by the previous government, a government which cancelled all employment programs, a government which took no initiatives in training or in providing ability to develop new ideas and innovations. On the other hand, we have been trying to do this in the very real recognition that we have fiscal restraint. But we cannot go whole hog, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party wants us to do. We have to provide a balance between what we can spend and what we must do in terms of maintaining some hedge against inflation.
No one on this side has ever tried to say that what we are doing is absolutely perfect at all times. But we are making a good and effective effort. If members of this House would support the Minister of Finance in the kinds of proposals he is putting forward which are designed to cut into that inflationary cycle, to provide the bite for the kinds of cost increases we have, to provide for the kinds of incentives needed to gain the co-operation of the business community and to get the unions to start restraining their own demands, then I think we can begin to beat inflation in Canada.
The Economy
