subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has chosen at this time to vacate the House. I was going to mention it was rather fortunate that three ministers of the Crown were here who I felt hold a tremendous responsibility for the plight in which we Canadians find ourselves. I refer, of course, to the emperor's triumverate. We have the 20 per cent kid, sometimes referred to as the Minister of Finance, who has decided to leave; we have Dr. Doolittle, sometimes referred to as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray); and then we have old ironclad himself, sometimes referred to as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). I hope that the 20 per cent kid will, in due course, read my remarks and take to heart some of the things I am going to say.
I rise to participate in this debate at a time when our inflation level is approaching 14 per cent, when we have a prime interest rate of approximately 20 per cent, and when our dollar is literally limp in relation to the American dollar. I find it most strange that we have such a complacent, rather indifferent attitude on the part of the government to the problems which this nation is facing. In fact, it is worse than that. It is

May 14, 1981
The Economy
not just indifferent, it is a tendency to want to distort the facts, to mislead the public into thinking that what is in fact true today is somehow not the way it appears. Surely Mr. Speaker, you will recall only yesterday when the 20 per cent kid rose to speak on this subject, and as reported at page 9551 of Hansard said:
I am not ready to engage in a debate about the historic causes of inflation in this country.
Frankly, I do not blame the Minister of Finance for not wanting to get into that debate because I know he would agree how damning it is of his government's own record. Having said that, the minister went on to say the following, talking about governments:
-especially in the early part of the seventies, were strongly pursuing expansionary policies and adding to their deficits, the public and all political parties generally supported that type of fiscal policy.
I was not here before 1972 but I have been in this House since 1972. I find it astounding that a minister of the Crown would stand up and mislead everyone, not only this House but the Canadian public, by suggesting that the deficit financing which Liberal governments engaged in during the 1970s was agreed to by all parties, because that is just not true. For four of those years I was financial spokesperson for the official opposition. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and I know you will agree, that I repeatedly, on behalf of my party, pleaded with the government to come to its senses, to cut back on its spending and reduce its deficit. I did that because the country was falling into a pattern which was going to produce the same inflationary atmosphere in which we are now living.
It is one thing for the government to have made mistakes in the past, to have led us into the bewildering situation that we have today; but for the government now to be trying to create the impression that we did it all together, that we all agreed to the type of economic approach which has led to the present inflationary pressures, is totally untrue. It is not worthy of the Minister of Finance and I would ask him to withdraw that type of comment.
One might say that three years ago it was all right for the government to say, "Let us try this thing called gradualism which has been recommended by our officials. Let us try this process where we are told that if we allow interest rates to rise, somehow or another that will eventually dampen the economy and lower inflation." I can understand the government of the day accepting that kind of thinking. But at some point, surely, we have to ask when the experiment will end.
We should also conclude that if the remedy is wrong then it must be corrected. For example, in April, 1978, the chartered bank prime rate was 8.5 per cent. In fact, it had ranged from the 6.75 per cent to the 8.5 per cent level through November, 1970, to April, 1978. In short, we never had the type of interest rate structure during that period with which we are now living. In fact, right up to May, 1978, the rate was still 8.75 per cent. On May 30 it rose to 9 per cent.
Since May, 1978, under the inspiration of the present government, the prime rates of our chartered banks have risen from 8.75 per cent to the present 19.5 per cent. They have
more than doubled. One would have thought that if the spirit or the theory behind gradualism and rising interest rates was to work and curb inflation, we would now be seeing the fruits of it. But we find that inflation in 1977, judged by the CPI, was 8 per cent; in 1978 it was 9 per cent; in 1979 it was 9.1 per cent; in 1980 it was 11.2 per cent; and currently it is running at 13.9 per cent on the minister's own admission. At least, that has been the rate since he brought in his last budget. Notwithstanding the interest rate explosion of rates doubling in that period, we also have an inflation level which has risen more than 50 per cent during the same period.
Can the government not come to its senses? Can it not at least step back and say, "We have become the mad scientists who have put forth a theory which obviously is not working; we must adjust our theory"? In short, economists from coast to coast are now saying that there is a better way, that there should be credit controls or that some type of more direct approach to the entire financial economic system is needed as opposed to this rather arbitrary, "Let's have higher rates of interest in the hope that they will cool out inflation".
The reason I emphasize this is that I feel we in the House somehow become removed from the reality of what we are talking about. It is easy to talk about 10 per cent or 15 per cent per annum inflation, or, as Dr. Campbell of Wood Gundy Limited said, that we are heading for 20 per cent if the government does not come to its senses as far as inflation is concerned. But the reality for the average home owner or average consumer who must shop for groceries is very much more vivid.
Since 1970 I have kept a record of the cost of what we call a shopping basket in my riding which contains 15 different items one might buy when shopping on the week end at a local store. This record is telling of the hardships being inflicted upon the Canadian public. I would like to review how those items have soared in price due to government policy or lack of policy concerning inflation. For example, in November, 1970 the 15 items had a total cost of $9.97. That is what it cost a consumer to buy a 15-ounce package of Special K, a three-quart jug of 2 per cent milk, a one-pound sirloin steak, a dozen grade A eggs, a pound of Maxwell House coffee, two 19-ounce tins of Libby's pork and beans, two ten-ounce tins of Campbell's tomato soup, ten pounds of white sugar, six ten-ounce tins of coke, a 48-ounce tin of Mitchell apple juice, a pound of centre cut pork chops, a pound of centre cut ham, eight eight-ounce slices of Kraft Canadian cheese, a 12-ounce jar of Billy Bee honey, and a one-pound package of chicken breasts.
If one goes down to the local store to buy those same articles-and some of them are now expressed in metric, to make it more confusing-they will cost today $34.65. This is a jump of 247 per cent since November, 1970. Faced with that, surely the government of the day must accept the responsibility for this crisis. It is time that it quit playing political games. It is time for Dr. Doolittle over there to do something to help the poor, downtrodden Canadian who is overtaxed and over
May 14, 1981

regulated, rather than pompously saying, "I am the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; I am a man of great authority".
I have touched upon the cost of those items, but we must realize that a 15-ounce package of Special K which cost 56 cents in November, 1970, now costs $1.99, thanks to the policies of the government; a three-quart jug of 2 per cent milk which then cost 67 cents, thanks to the emperor who has ruled the country for 12 years now costs $2.97.

I remind hon. members what we are debating. It is a resolution of my leader which reads as follows:
The Economy
That this House deplores the record high interest rates imposed on Canadians by the Liberal government which together with double-digit inflation and slow economic growth are causing acute hardship and human suffering for Canadians-
Today we are debating what we really believe, that the inflationary spiral, the spiral of rising interest rates and the lack of real growth in the country, do not have to continue. If the government does not change its ways, if it does not do something effective, the prices of those commodities will continue to rise. I should like to refer to what the prices of those commodities will be in 1985. I have not gone back and then ahead ten years; I have simply taken a look at what will be the prices of these various commodities four years down the road if the government does not get a handle on inflation soon. We will find in 1985 that a three-quart jug of 2 per cent milk will be selling for $6.53.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext: Tell us about Billy Bee honey.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
It sold for 67 cents in 1970 and it will be selling for $6.53 in 1985, if the last four years of inflationary price increases on 2 per cent milk continue for another four years. The hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson), of all places, asks about Billy Bee honey. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if that hon. member partakes of Bill Bee honey, that is the sweetest thing about him. A 12-ounce jar of Billy Bee honey which sold for 31 cents in November, 1970, will sell for $2.10 four years from now if something is not done. I point out for example, that sirloin steak, which cost 99 cents a pound in November, 1970, and which now costs $4.69, will cost $13.88 per pound by 1985 if we do not halt the price increases we are referring to in our motion. We have a situation now where the apple juice I referred to earlier, which cost 34 cents in November, 1970, and which currently costs $1.13, will cost $1.61 four years down the road. This is why I urge all members to take a serious look at our motion instead of meekly sitting on the government benches accepting what has been told them by their masters. If they cannot take a serious look at this during this debate, then I suggest they do so in the discussions which should ensue concerning the plight facing this nation.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are trying to attract the attention of the House. I do not know whether it is because of my time or whether it is because you wish to make an announcement. In any event, I await your words.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly would not vote for such a motion because, frankly, it does not hold up under any kind of scrutiny at all, particularly when one remembers what was done by the party opposite when it formed the government.
I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on this particular subject since I think it is a matter of serious concern to all Canadians, whether it be 1970 or in the present circumstances. We are all concerned about what is happening at the present time with respect to the economy and what the impact will be on us, our children and our children's children. We have a heavy responsibility to do more than engage in what is, in my view, simply condemning rhetoric.
In answer to a question earlier this week, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said he would await with interest some constructive criticism from members opposite to help in this Fight against inflation. I, too, as chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs would have welcomed suggestions about how the economy might be improved, about what actions we might take to curb inflation and about methods which could be used to bring down interest rates. I would have been happy to weigh those views and suggestions and, where I could agree with them, to press them upon the Minister of Finance of this government. But, Mr. Speaker, I have waited in vain. I heard a great deal of rhetoric and condemnation but very little in the way of positive actions which could be taken to reduce inflation in the country.
I listened to the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I thought he would have given us something a little better and more self-serving than the suggestion that we should reintroduce his budget. His was a budget which was defeated not only in the House of Commons but in the country when put to a vote. What kind of a recommendation is that? It is a kind of stand pat suggestion which was rejected by this House and by the people of Canada.
Listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
-we wage the battle against inflation, Mr. Speaker. It is to save those and to defend those who are having their savings destroyed; those who are so essential to society that we need to save, and see that their savings don't go down the drain because governments are unwilling to fight inflation. That is what high interest rates are all about, because the world, the western industrialized world,
has not conducted its economic and monetary system properly, so that we are in a period of high inflation.
That high inflation has to be dealt with, and that is our main enemy if we are to have any kind of progressive society in the future here in Canada. That is why interest rates are high. Why are interest rates high? They are high because we have an inflation rate ... annualized during September of 14 per cent. Because our dollar has fallen in value to 83 cents or 84 cents, those imports are costing us more and adding to our inflation. Therefore, we have to try to protect the Canadian dollar, to protect it from falling much further because of the effect that will have on the inflation we are importing from the United States.
We do not have high interest rates because this government wants high interest rates. That is not our policy. As politicians we do not want high interest rates. The people do not want high interest rates. Nobody wants high interest rates, so it is not a policy of the government to have high interest rates, it is a condition that the government cannot do anything about at the moment. It is not through choice.
Those are not the words of our Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker; those are the words of the hon. member for St. John's West when he was minister of finance and responsible for guiding the economy of this country. It was at a time when he recognized the problem and defended the impact of high interest rates.
The people of Canada know that the fight against inflation will be long and difficult. Inflation has been caused by a series of events and the Canadian public, fortunately, are sophisticated enough to appreciate that it is not solely the government which is to blame for the problems we face today with respect to inflation. There have been many who have contributed to inflation. For that reason the fight against it will be difficult.
But it is not a Fight from which we can back away. The people of Canada know that the quadrupling of the price of oil by OPEC and subsequent increases have played a major role for the worst in our economy. Canadians who live under the banner of rising expectations make the fight against inflation very difficult. American interest rates impact in a monstrous way and now even Germany, in effect, is saying to the United States, "Cool it!". Germany is telling the United States to watch what it is doing to the economies of the industrialized world. Not just Canada is suffering from this impact, Germany is now speaking out and indicating its concern with the impact of high interest rates on its economy.
Whenever we have unfettered demands for unreasonable wage and salary increases we have trouble of the most serious nature. I am happy to say that union leaders are more reasonable and understanding now than I have ever known to be the case before. However, they too have a constituency. They have an obligation to represent the people who have elected them to a position of trust and to a position of looking after their interests. Those companies which charge what the market will bear, rather than setting themselves a standard where they would get a reasonable return on investments, do great harm to the economy. All of these factors can be shown to have a substantial impact on any attempt to control inflation.
I believe the Governor of the Bank of Canada is right to be concerned about the strength of the Canadian dollar which now fluctuates somewhere between 82 cents and 85 cents U.S.
May 14, 1981

Those who buy goods from abroad recognize that a weaker dollar would push inflation beyond tolerable levels. I have heard the comment, "Why don't you just say, okay, no more increase in interest rates, or pass a law to reduce interest rates?" Where would the dollar plummet? Who in this chamber charged with the responsibility of deciding would make that particular move? Only someone totally irresponsible or one who does not have to face the music of the plummeting dollar.

speechtext: That is what Herb Gray said a year ago.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Once, on a visit to the OECD, I asked a couple of economists and two politicians from other countries who were interested in this subject and involved with the finance departments of their own countries: "Tomorrow, if you were named the economic czar of Canada and had the uncontrolled right to take action, what would you do for us, as Canadians, to control inflation?" Not one of their suggestions had practical, political credibility. There were ideas such as closing down all the inefficient industries; to force some corporations to join together to rationalize, to give each a particular share of the market; to do away with unemployment insurance, that without it people would find work because they would have to and they would be satisfied just to be working. Suggestions were made to stop DREE, as it forces corporations to locate where it is economically inadvisable to conduct business; to raise taxes to cover our deficit. I wonder, if that kind of action was taken, raise taxes on whom?
They said we should encourage foreign investment and close down FIRA. They said we should raise the price of stamps to cover whatever it cost to run the Post Office. If management in the Post Office saw that they would lose business by being inefficient, they would work together to become more efficient so that the cost of mail and parcel delivery would decrease. I told those particular advisers that I was thankful they were not the economic czars of Canada. I told them that in Canada, instead of having a revolution of rising expectations, we would have a revolution of a different kind.
Because we are in the Parliament of Canada, we should be making suggestions about what the federal government can do to assume its responsibility in its fight against inflation. Much pleasure has been taken by the opposition in tweaking the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for saying on one occasion that we had wrestled inflation to the ground. I would like to remind the opposition, and maybe the Prime Minister as well, that wrestling is often, at best, two out of three falls. Maybe the battle is even at the present time and we still have a job of work to do if we are going into that particular ring.
At the present time the deficit is barely manageable, and for it to become much larger is unthinkable. So one area we must look to is reducing our demands on the taxpayers' dollar. Not too often do I hear MPs suggesting we should cut expenditures, or at least in any amount which would have a significant impact on the deficit. I have heard expressions like "a stimulative deficit", "spend more money", "use more money", "do more protecting", to use this money and call it a stimulative
The Economy
deficit. My concern there is that if it does not stimulate, then we have nothing but a larger deficit, again working to the detriment of the Canadian public and certainly of the Canadian economy.
I hear from time to time that certain protections should be put in place, and it has a nice ring to it. But protection costs taxpayers dollars. I was not here at the time the hon. member for St. John's West introduced his mortgage deductibility plan. However, I studied the idea of it and I talked to people who saw it in place in the United States; after all, my riding is a border community. I was very pleased to note that we did not adopt that particular program because there would have been a built-in cost factor which we would have found very difficult to unload at some time in the future. I think it would have been reprehensible for Parliament to have adopted that particular program, knowing the cost of it and knowing that even though it is really basically unacceptable to the government of the United States, now that it is locked into it there is no way that it can get out.
We did take some action in the areas of most vulnerability. The guaranteed income supplement was increased immediately after this Parliament resumed. I think that was an appropriate move. I would like to see the government give some thought to issuing tax-free bonds where money derived from that particular source could be used for government projects. We should be looking at that area, and I have made that suggestion to the Minister of Finance.
I would like to join with a portion of the comments made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I do not think they should be forced to do it at the present time, but I think banks and trust companies must look to their social responsibilities in this Canadian society. Mortgages become due, and "boom", immediately up goes the interest rate. A company which has made a substantial amount of money as a result of someone who has paid on a mortgage for five, ten or 15 years should surely let that individual know that he is a good creditor who can be depended on, and that he has given no difficulty because he has kept up his payments. Surely these institutions have a social, moral and, for that matter, should possibly have a legal obligation to see to it that they protect the customers they encourage to come in and borrow funds, and from whom they have made a significant profit. They must face up to that particular social responsibility.
When one is in a one-industry town and there is a major strike, mortgage companies, not because they want to but because they really have no alternative, must find a method not to foreclose on mortgages, giving those who are on strike a little time instead of demanding that the full backlog be paid up immediately. When a strike lasts for six months or a year or some time-frame like that, a way must be found to accommodate those who are on strike. If these companies do not do so, they know that they are acting at their peril because when those people are back to work they will no longer deal with that particular institution. They do it not because they want to, but because they have to.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
I think banks must be reminded that it is not a computer print-out with which they are dealing but people. I am not as much concerned with showing a large profit at a time of difficulty as I am with convincing banks and trust companies that they have an obligation in tough times to see to it that they do what they can to help, particularly their steady customers and those from whom they have made substantial amounts of money. This is particularly true when they are trampling on their hopes, dreams and aspirations which are completely shattered for the sake of the few dollars which they could not come up with, even though they have come up with money over the last five, ten or 15 years. There comes a time when the Canadian public says that enough is enough, and they will put pressure on politicians to say that banks must accept this responsibility.
I think the banks should be reminded that in the provinces landlords were too tough on tenants, with the result that the provinces moved in with rent controls and provisions in landlord and tenants acts to protect tenants. I think they have probably gone too far in some instances; but the legislatures and the politicians had to react. I say to the banks and trust companies, be careful; people will only be pushed so far. Then they will push their politicians to do in the short run what they may see as necessary but which we might very well know will be counterproductive in the long run. If they do not recognize their social obligation, they will be acting at their peril.
Naturally, to help the economy we must come to an agreement with respect to the price of oil and gas in Canada. We have to have an agreement between the producing provinces and the federal government. I am happy to see we are prepared to make concessions to try to arrive at some form of agreement on pricing which will not totally decimate the people who have to buy the particular product. At the same time it will give a fair rate of return to the people who are doing the producing and to the producing provinces.
It seems to me that what is taking place now is good, that the officials are meeting, and we are at least talking about the same set of figures. At the federal level we have a tendency to say that the split for a barrel of oil is 45, 45 and 10, and the provincial government says that that is not true because there are other taxes and benefits which we at the federal level derive which makes that figure inappropriate. Let us get the figure down and agreed upon. Surely that is step one.
We should then say to industry, which wants to get back working, which wants to go on exploring, which wants to expand, "You will derive a certain figure from a barrel of oil and that is the bottom line. That money will be available to you." For the balance, let the federal and provincial governments work out some form of agreement but not hold up progress, so that these people can work.
I am proud of the fact that the federal government saw fit to make $40 million available to keep one particularly large project operating until, I believe, June 1, in order to see if some settlement could not be reached prior to that time. The
pressure is on; concessions will have to be made. I know that at the federal level we are prepared to do this. I am satisfied with the minister when he says he will move in that direction. I hope we can expect the same kind of co-operation from the producing provinces.
There is one other area of pricing that I should like to deal with. We have already indicated in the case of the tar sands and heavy oils that we are prepared to go to $37 per barrel, plus an indexing factor. That may not be enough but it strikes me that it is a substantial amount of money. Surely that is an area in which there can be negotiation. Maybe that figure is fine at the moment; to my way of thinking it seems to be adequate as the bottom line, given the fact that there is a built-in index.
My colleague from the riding adjacent to mine has indicated that he would like to see a two or three-price system; one price for the heavy oils and tar sands products, one for the ordinary oil, and more funding made available to the marginal wells. That would put a lot of people back to work on those wells because they would then be economically viable.
I note your indication that my time is about up, Mr. Speaker. I should just like to repeat what I said at the beginning, that rhetoric will not bring down inflation. We must all recognize that the solution is with us, that each of us in our own sector has a responsibility to do what we can to alleviate it. We must give protection to vulnerable members of our society, as we have done with the guaranteed income supplement. I think we must also give more money to bodies like the Farm Credit Corporation.
At the government level we must learn to say no unless it can be shown that the expenditure of more money will involve an investment which will be beneficial to the economy of the country and to all Canadians.
I do not envy the Minister of Finance in his very difficult and perplexing role. I know that he is sincere in his concern for his fellow Canadians. He is an individual who has taken on an almost impossible task and is doing what I think is a superb job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government's complacency in regard to economic issues is clearly illustrated by the agenda which it has placed before Parliament since this session began.
The government rejoices when its bad record at job creation in April compares favourably with its worse record in March, but this brings little comfort to the families of 886,000 unemployed Canadians.
The high interest policy of the government, which is now counterproductive and is contributing directly to increases in prices, has destroyed home building and condemned thousands of Canadians to renting expensive apartments with the certain knowledge that the rents will go even higher.
This government stubbornly refuses to bring in legislation to permit Canadians to deduct their mortgage interest from their
May 14, 1981

income tax, as the leader of the Progressive Conservative government did. It will, however, continue to allow the wealthiest industries in this country to deduct their interest payments from their income for tax purposes.
The economic recovery of our nation and the elimination of areas that suffer from regional disparity requires a plan. We need a national industrial strategy, and a piece of the action, at long last, should go to the Atlantic provinces.
The battle with regional disparity in Atlantic Canada will be won or lost on the industrial front. The development of secondary manufacturing is the top priority for the economic recovery of the Atlantic provinces. Secondary manufacturing must be upgraded, more specialized and more efficient. The benefits to the Atlantic provinces and the rest of the country are obvious.
At this point in time the Atlantic account, in terms of federal expenditures, shows that the Government of Canada spends $5 billion more each year in the Atlantic provinces than it recovers in revenues. It is therefore in the Atlantic provinces that a new industrial capacity, in terms of its impact on the totality of the nation, would be most beneficial. If we expand the industrial base, then we expand the revenue base for provincial governments and enable them to become less dependent on equalization and transfer payments. This would require fewer federal dollars and would be of direct benefit to every taxpayer in Canada.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) can mount an effective argument in persuading large industrial taxpayers to consider the Atlantic provinces in terms of their future expansion. It is in their interest, indeed in everybody's interest, to develop a broader tax base in Atlantic Canada in order to whittle away at transfer payments.
In terms of development, we have to ask ourselves where we are going to be in 1990 and in the year 2000. I want Atlantic Canada to be standing on its own two feet and making a net contribution to Canada, and I believe it will take strong financial incentives and moral suasion to bring this about.
The 50 per cent tax incentive credit that the government has recently brought in is a step in the right direction, but it has one glowing deficiency in that it does not apply to all of the Altantic provinces. Specifically excluded from the incentive is the area in New Brunswick with the greatest industrial potential for manufacturing plants, and that is the Moncton-Saint John-Fredericton triangle.
Another incentive recommended by the New Brunswick Development Institute and ignored by the government is the 30 per cent tax incentive for labour costs in manufacturing plants for the first three years of operation. This is intended to offset the training costs for employees in new plants at new jobs. The greatest benefit of these two incentives is that they would not cost the federal treasury anything. They would only postpone the tax-paying liability of companies that do not now exist and so do not pay taxes; in fact, taxpayers would be
The Economy
created. This would meet the requirement mentioned earlier by an hon. member opposite.
We need strong incentives and these are important, but so is the element of persuasion.
The government missed the chance to contribute to a more balanced economic growth in western and eastern Canada when it signed the auto pact. The government failed to use the opportunity to persuade the automobile giants of the importance of locating some aspect of their industrial empires in eastern and western Canada.
The social benefits of 500 jobs would have far greater impact in Altantic Canada than anywhere else in our nation. The taxes derived from 500 taxpayers would nibble away at the need for equalization grants and federal transfer payments. Where nearly one dollar out of two spent by governments in Atlantic Canada can be traced back to the federal government, there is a real incentive for an enlightened federal government to look at this proposition very seriously.
Secondary manufacturing plants have a great development impact because they buy goods and services, employ a large number of people and stimulate other service and support industries.
I want to pay tribute to DREE and to those who have worked hard to establish our industrial parks in Atlantic Canada. These industrial parks have made a contribution to development, but regrettably more often than not we find very few manufacturing plants in our industrial parks. Space is taken more by warehouses, wholesale and commercial undertakings which, while they are very important, do not create the number of jobs that a manufacturing plant would. In order to attract manufacturing plants, strong incentives are essential and so is moral suasion exercised by the Prime Minister and the ministers of the Crown.
In order to create a climate attractive to industry and development we need many things. One of them is a sound transportation policy. The maritime provinces through their governments working with DREE and the Department of Transport have taken some good steps in this direction, but there is much yet to be done.
The blueprint for the development of the port of Saint John has to be followed aggressively, and a similar blueprint for the development of the port of Halifax has to be put in place and acted upon. The significant transfer of shipping from Halifax to Montreal is a horror story that should never have been told. It should have been nipped in the bud by the alert ministers of the Crown from Nova Scotia and the Minister of Transport.
The retrenchment of rail and express services in the maritime provinces is a betrayal of one of the fundamental reasons for our entry into confederation. This government of contradictions that, on the one hand, enshrines the principles of equalization in our Constitution and at the same time sets in motion a parliamentary task force to examine federal-provincial fiscal arrangements with a view to reducing them, is now

May 14, 1981
The Economy
talking openly about putting its contribution to the improvement of the transportation systems in the maritimes in an envelope. It will essentially pass the buck to the maritime governments themselves to decide which mode will get the least. Why? Because the federal government has no policy, it has no strategy, it has no plan, and it will not take the time to sit down with the provincial governments involved and work one out. It would rather bunch its meagre efforts in one bundle than allocate the funds in accordance with a meaningful plan so the cutbacks in its reduced efforts will not be so apparent.
In Prince Edward Island the federal-provincial development agreement is moving ahead like a fly with a wooden leg walking across a saucer of molasses. In New Brunswick, the subsidiary agreement to provide federal assistance for small business incentive programs has expired and not been renewed. The highway subsidiary agreement has expired and has not been renewed. The tourism agreement has expired and has not been renewed. The fisheries agreement has not expired because it has never been completed. These are good programs. They create a climate attractive to industry. They should not have been allowed to expire. We are now two months into the current fiscal year and without the agreements, the funds allocated for the programs cannot be spent. This is not good planning. It is not good administration. The government is not doing its homework and is not operating efficiently.
I would like to identify some individual projects for the government to consider as it contemplates its next budget. Most of these projects will not involve expenditures which have not already been contemplated, but would, I believe, focus them in a more meaningful way.
The forestry complex to be located at the university of New Brunswick would put meaning and purpose into research and development for the vital forest industry in New Brunswick. It is an urgent necessity that has attracted the interest and support of two of the more able ministers of the Crown, and I hope that their enlightenment will soon be shared by the Treasury Board. This project would give industry a window on research that would be very valuable for the whole Atlantic region.
I would like to see the practice of contracting out research and development projects of large magnitude continue, but I would like to suggest that very large contracts in this field could be used as an inducement to our high technology industry to promote a more balanced growth across the country. I realize it is not possible to suggest that an industry should locate in an area in order to get a grant, and then find out that it is unable to sustain its production after that, but I do suggest that it is a factor which, combined with other elements, should be considered. In this regard, I would like to see the appropriate ministers of the Crown set up an interdepartmental committee to address the prospect of giving a development dimension to research and development in our high technology industry in Canada.
I would also like to see the Department of Supply and Services take another look at its procurement policy with
respect to foreign aid. Right now the department centres its bidding process on goods delivered to the port of Montreal because it is from that port that it ships its supplies to developing countries. I would like to see this practice varied once in awhile and the ports of Saint John and Halifax used as the gathering point to give a better chance to suppliers in Atlantic Canada to participate in these large orders.
Before closing I would like to touch upon two development opportunities in my riding. In the town of Oromocto we have a large number of vacant married quarters for armed forces personnel stationed at Canadian Forces Base Gagetown. The changing complexion of the armed forces which sees more single persons than has been the case has resulted in the depopulation of the town of Oromocto which was created originally by the Department of National Defence. This model town was originally designed as a combination of civilian and military personnel and for many years operated under the direction of a commission, with a majority of its officers being appointed by the Department of National Defence. Over a period of time it has evolved and acquired the status of a town. It now elects its own government, the same as other Canadian towns.
I feel that the Department of National Defence still has a moral obligation as the largest taxpayer in the town and as its founder to do all it can for the well-being of the municipality and the people who live there.
The depopulation of the town of Oromocto has created a serious problem in the school system, and commercial and professional people in the town do not have the same potential as they had before the population decreased. Strong efforts are being made to attract industry to the town, and I think the government of Canada should do all it can to assist it.
Specifically I would like to see the Department of National Defence give serious consideration to stationing more personnel in the town and make a greater effort to fulfil its obligation, both to the armed forces and to the people of central New Brunswick.
In New Brunswick we have one of the most beautiful natural attractions in the world in the Saint John river which divides the city of Fredericton and is bordered by a very attractive green. I would like to see an in-depth study done of the recreation potential of the river. Environment officials tell me that it is essentially pollution free, although an incident last winter would have to be checked out. Any such study would have to check carefully all the safety factors. The question of fluctuating water levels and its effect on safe swimming, boating and skating would have to be given very careful consideration. The topography and condition of the river bottom and the possibility of moving in sand to locate some beaches are other factors.
Now that the two government wharfs have been removed for the access roads leading to the new bridge, the question of a new wharf to permit boating and river boat cruises has arisen.
One very attractive proposal for the development of river boat cruises along the Saint John river is taking shape at this
May 14, 1981

moment and it has my support. I think the development of natural resources such as the Saint John river for our own people as well as tourists would make New Brunswick a very attractive site for developments of all kinds.
I mentioned this last project because it has a very small federal content and would essentially be developed by two other levels of government. However, it is important for us as members of Parliament to identify projects which can be accomplished with staff and resources that are now in place. It can make our areas in Canada more attractive for development.
The government has suggested that the opposition is using this opportunity just to be negative and to expose the government's frailties. I have chosen to lay before the government some positive suggestions which I hope will attract its attention. They would involve very little in the way of more investment on the part of the government, in fact none that has not already been contemplated in the estimates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in this debate on the severe increase in interest rates. In so doing, I would like to address two major points. First, I would like to sum up the facts as they relate to our present economic circumstances. Second, I want to respond to the challenge presented by the Leader of the New Democratic Party to deal in a positive and constructive way with some of the alternatives which have been presented to us, not only by his party but by the official opposition.
First, it must be recognized that Canada, more than any other nation in the world, is dependent for its economic well-being, economic health and economic fundamentals on world trade and international capital flow. More than 25 per cent of our gross national product comes from exports, and this is a higher figure than even for Japan. We are not an isolated nation. We cannot set out to conduct our economic affairs on the basis that we are in watertight compartments, or that we are an island unto ourselves. World economic realities are there and always will be, and the moment we as Canadians ignore those economic realities and start to look inward we will begin to suffer severe economic consequences.
What are some of these facts which relate to our present economic condition? I want to set these forth in the light of the seven major countries in OECD. These are Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States, Italy and Japan. Let us look at the way in which Canada relates in its economic performance to those specific countries. I want to do this within the context of the theory which has been put forward that other countries have had to go to world prices in oil, have gone to world prices in oil and have been able to digest those prices within their own domestic economies.
Yes, they have digested world prices for energy but at what price; what price have they had to pay? I want to look at this because, in looking at the facts, we will see that since 1973 they have digested these higher prices for oil at great cost to
The Economy
themselves. Let us look at this in terms of unemployment rates. Of these seven OECD countries including Canada, Canada is the only one to have had a decline in unemployment every year since 1978. We are the only country with a lower unemployment rate today than in 1978.
Let us look at manufacturing employment, and manufacturing employment is part of what we are promoting through our industrial strategy. Since 1973, of the seven OECD countries, Canada has had the highest increase in the number of manufacturing jobs. Only Canada and the United States have had an increase in the number of people employed in manufacturing.
Let us look at total employment, and I believe it is important to look at this because when we are dealing with employment we are dealing with human beings and the dignity of individuals who have the opportunity to work. Unemployment is more than a statistic. Unemployment is a tragedy when it occurs in the human family. This is why we have to look at these figures.
In terms of total employment since 1973, when the increase in OPEC prices occurred, Canada has had the highest growth rate in total employment of those seven OECD countries. It has been over 3 per cent a year. The next highest was in the U.S. with 2.5 per cent. All of the others have had a growth rate of less than 1 per cent. In fact, Germany, often held out to us as the paragon of economic virtue, had one million fewer workers employed in 1980 than it did in 1973. That is the price Germany has had to pay for digesting world energy pricing.
In terms of economic growth, between 1973 and 1980 all top OECD countries have had a reduced rate of economic growth. We do not like this but it is a fact. We have all suffered, but Canada's decline in economic growth has been less than that of all those other OECD countries.
Let us look at our merchandise trade balance. Canada is the only OECD country to have an increase in its merchandise trade balance in every year since 1978. As a matter of fact, last year Canada's merchandise trade balance surplus was higher than that of Japan.

speechtext: Oh, don't be absurd.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext: The hon. member opposite should look at the figures. I would be happy to give him those figures released by OECD.

speechtext: I don't care who released them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
In the last 12 months our merchandise trade surplus was $6 billion, and in Japan it was $4.7 billion.
Exchange rates have come under pressure throughout the world. There has been a decline. The French franc, the Deutschmark and the yen have declined from between 5 per cent to 12 per cent in the last three years, with the rapid increase in OPEC prices, against the U.S. dollar, while the Canadian dollar has remained constant.
Let us consider inflation rates. None of us wants or likes inflation. We all think inflation is too high. This is why we are

May 14, 1981
The Economy
taking responsible measures to try to bring it down, but all of these OECD countries have had an inflationary increase of approximately 3 per cent. Our inflationary increase has not been out of line with those of our major trading partners. I can say the same for central government deficits. They again have followed that line.
What do these figures indicate to us in the real world? None of us like huge fiscal deficits, none of us like high inflation rates, and none of us like high interest rates, but what these mean is that we have not been using these fiscal deficit tools in a totally unconstructive way. We have been using them to promote employment, create jobs for people and give dignity to families. We have been using them to promote economic growth. None of us is proud of present circumstances, but I think, when we look at them within the context of the real world, we have to say perhaps that we can do better, and we have to find ways to do better. However, our performance has been better than that of any of the other major countries that count in this area.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Let me accept the challenge put to us by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) to respond to the alternatives presented to us. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) during the question period on Tuesday said that a speedy energy agreement would help us to protect Canadians against downward pressure on the Canadian dollar. This must be a price that is related to the cost of becoming self-sufficient in energy, and not a price tied to an artificial "X" per cent, whatever that may be.

That is the basis for negotiating a reasonable agreement with the provinces which is not artificially tied to some price unrelated to Canadian needs, Canadian supplies and, particularly, the needs of Canadian consumers.

from the United States. The interest equalization tax was designed to penalize foreigners who were coming into the United States to borrow. I think we have to look at the example of what is happening in the United States. However, I do not think any of us should ignore the opportunity to re-examine new ideas and concepts at this time. I welcome the receptive attitude of our Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and our party toward exploring these new ideas because all of us are engaged in the search to create a better economy for Canadians.

I think all of us agree that the real question with respect to bringing interest rates down involves bringing inflation down, and that involves over the long run-and there is only one way to do it-increased productivity among Canadians. Another major question we must face is whether we are going to benefit under our industrial strategy, foreign owned or only Canadian owned.
Another problem we have to address in coming to a resolution of this question is what type of activities we want to encourage. In this area I suggest we want to encourage export-oriented industries using world product mandate techniques, and I say this in response to the hon. member opposite who asked, "Where are the markets?" The other types of activities it is incumbent upon us to encourage are research and development. Without increased research and development, be it in the white collar area or in manufacturing, we will not be competitive on a world basis.
There is a number of means we can examine in the area of developing an industrial strategy. How are we going to do it? Are we going to have increased bureaucracies in which government officials determine who is a winner, who is a loser, who gets what and who does not? In some areas we might have to. We might find, after consultation, that that is the most effective way, but I suggest we will find that the most effective way will be to pick our winners and look at the Income Tax Act. Who are the people who are making profits and who have demonstrated their ability? What about incentives for those people who have demonstrated ability and want to reinvest in Canada?
In terms of our industrial strategy, we could also look at the utilization of FIRA. FIRA is an instrument by which we can encourage greater use of the world product mandate. This is where we produce in Canada a limited run of goods of one type and of a similar kind. We cannot produce 20 brands of refrigerators in Canada, but we can produce two and sell them around the world. That is the way we get economies of scale. To my way of thinking, that is part of the industrial strategy and part of the forward thinking we are doing.

May 14, 1981

Let us recognize that under our industrial strategy we can build on the success we have. Such successes are Mitel, ATCO, Dominion Trucks and our resource-oriented companies. We do have opportunities. We need to have co-operation between the government and the private sector. I am not ashamed to look at the example of the minister of international trade and investment in Japan. Japan encourages active cooperation between the private sector, financial institutions and business. This involves the creative use of all the talents of government and the private sector. That is the way we make winners in the capitalist system. That is the way we make winners in our economy based on the free enterprise system.
There are many challenges before us. I wish hon. members opposite had taken more time to discuss in detail positive alternatives because I believe these alternatives are within our grasp. I am proud to be part of a party which is actively seeking out those solutions and dealing with them.
