subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret the circumstances which require me to participate in this important debate that reflects the government's absolute incompetence and its mismanagement of our national economy. We are faced with record high interest rates now in excess of 20 per cent, double-digit inflation in the order of 12.5 per cent and, worst of all, the government has produced no significant programs. In particular, it has not produced its long-promised industrial development strategy in order to resolve the worsening economic crisis.
This evening I want to spend a few moments talking about my understanding of the causes of the problem and to dispel some of the myths we regularly hear from the other side. I want to talk about the impact of high interest rates and inflation upon the Canadian fishing industry, particularly on the west coast. Also I want to talk a little about some of the solutions we in this party see as being essential.
Canada is on a course of economic suicide because of the incompetent economic doodlers, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on down, who have set the country on a course toward economic disaster which may well be at least as severe as the great depression of the thirties. I believe high interest rates are but a symptom of a national disaster we are yet to confront.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) said that higher interest rates are needed to get inflation down, in order to get interest rates down. What illogical rubbish! The hon. member should know better. It just does not work that way. Higher interest rates do not create a situation leading to lower interest rates. In fact, in a situation where taxes are too high, business confidence is low and profit margins are slim, companies, businesses, fishermen and ordinary people in the country have no room in which to manoeuvre. There is no profit margin left, and the consequence is what some technical people might call a synergetic or cyclical effect: the higher the interest rate becomes, the higher the inflation rate becomes, and the higher the interest rate becomes again. Then there is an amplifying headlong deterioration of the economy, leading ultimately to a disastrous consequence.
Last week and again today the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) said that the Canadian worker is to blame, that he earns too much and he expects too much of this country. What nonsense! The minister cannot blame the wage earners; he cannot blame wives, spouses or children; he cannot blame farmers, fishermen, small businessmen, pensioners, widowers, widows or school teachers. Furthermore, the minister cannot blame the Americans or Ronald Reagan. That is the phoniest excuse of them all. I did some checking today and learned that on this very day mortgage rates in the United States are at 16 per cent. Last August they were 12 per cent or 13 per cent. In other words, mortgage rates in the United States have increased by some 3 per cent to 4 per cent since last August. By comparison, mortgage rates in Canada, as of today's hike in the prime lending rate, have increased from 13 per cent to some 21 per cent-an 8 per cent increase in nine months. The increase in mortgage rates in Canada is double that of the United States for the same period. It is neither correct nor honest to suggest the situation is otherwise. In fact, the wide fluctuations in the U.S. prime lending rate bear little relationship, if plotted against time, with the fluctuations in interest rates which represent a progressive rise in this country.
May 14, 1981

We cannot have a government continuing to misrepresent the truth to the Canadian people. The federal government causes inflation, and it knows as well as anyone else in this country that it does. As a consequence of inflation, we are faced with high interest rates. The Minister of Finance knows that, too. After all, who is overprinting the money supply? Who is incurring massive budgetary deficits of $100 billion plus? Who is borrowing against the future value of our natural resources, particularly those resources in western Canada upon which the federal government is so anxious to lay its hands? Who has tied up all of the people's money in Canada Savings Bonds and government pension funds, and then squandered it to pay ever mounting deficits? Who has forced all Canadian revenues, or at least $300 billion of those revenues, into real estate and housing because a capital gains tax was slapped on everything else, destroying the incentive to invest in business and entrepreneurial ventures, diverting that revenue into the housing market? Who has created a shortage of investment capital in this country by spending someone else's money on unnecessary programs of intervention by government into the private sector, by creating 400-plus Crown corporations, many of them unnecessary, by imposing a National Energy Program which confiscates resources and revenues and the free opportunities which private corporations in this country seek? Who has imposed red tape and overregulation upon the private sector of this country? Who is mortgaging the future and incurring bills which our children will have to pay, and how much does the interest payment amount to on those bills? In the present fiscal year it will amount to not $14 billion but something close to $20 billion which is needed to pay the interest to foreign and Canadian lenders on the deficits which this government has incurred. Why are funds fleeing south to seek refuge from the National Energy Program? Why are these funds fleeing south? Because there is a scarcity of oil and gas in the United States and investors are paid well for investing in oil and gas exploration in the U.S. That is where Canadian, American and other dollars are flooding to from this country.
There is another reason why the interest rates in this country must be as high as the government claims they must be. We are seeing the beginnings of industrial nationalization. As the Minister of Finance hinted this afternoon, there are other corporations which will be the next ones to be subjected to federal intervention. Perhaps banks, food stores, food chains, General Motors, farming and fishing industries will all be subject to nationalization if this government has its way. And the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) sitting opposite smiles. In the Department of Fisheries and Oceans alone there is a pervasive attempt, month after month, to try to take a bigger piece of the action from private sector fishing companies, which is something I will deal with later on.
So we have the choice between propping up the Canadian dollar in order to keep it at an 85 per cent par with the U.S. dollar or our interest rates will have to go higher and higher. The alternative is to allow the Canadian dollar to collapse. Why is the government afraid of a devalued dollar? Because
The Economy
the government must then bear the burden of responsibility for its own economic mismanagement. It must bear it directly instead of forcing that burden upon the backs and incomes of ordinary Canadians everywhere who are innocent in this tragic dilemma which our country faces. We have spent almost 12 months in this House frittering away time debating a constitutional initiative which is dividing our country and creating ill will everywhere when we should have been dealing with these important economic problems.
I submit that the Prime Minister and the government should call a first ministers' conference immediately, tell the premiers that they will put this power play aside and get on in a spirit of co-operation with resolving our important economic crisis.
When will the Minister of Finance admit that our national economic problems are a direct result of a government which spends itself into power and attempts to stay in power election after election by promising all kinds of goodies to the taxpayer who must ultimately pay for these extravagances? The Canadian economy is suffering from this spend-spend-spend mentality, an approach which leads to politically expedient solutions and ideological frivolity which started in the early seventies and which will continue as long as the people of this country allow it to continue.
There are no signs of restraint in the budget introduced by this government a year ago. It is high time a new budget was brought in which would show indications of restraints. If we had been in government in this present fiscal year with the Crosbie budget in effect, the national deficit would have been reduced to 14 per cent of the annual budgetary spending. Instead, it will be more than 20 per cent with the higher interest charges on our foreign deficit. It is now approaching 25 per cent, or a charge of some $20 billion for the interest we must pay on our national deficit. The reasons for this problem really have to do with the wasteful spending habits of this government-the Mirabel airports, the great "metri-Can" boondoggle which will cost small retail businesses across Canada more than half a billion dollars, $600 million, in order to buy new scales from foreign multinational companies. These are scales which will be imported and, therefore, have a negative effect on our balance of payments. We want to buy gas stations to pretend that we are somehow in charge of our own economic energy destiny. We want to print government documents in duplicate, back to back, in both official languages instead of printing half as many documents in two languages. That is an utterly ridiculous waste of valuable Canadian newsprint. We have a great Canada Week put on at the expense of millions of dollars of taxpayers' money, trying to bludgeon Canadians into a feeling of loyalty which should come from inside, not be forced on them by government propaganda. We have the concept of CBC-2 which is absolutely unnecessary at this point in time. We have the minister responsible for culture saying that we should forget about foreign aid and think about a new art gallery for Ottawa since that is more important than getting control of our economic destiny. There are DREE grants to fat cat friends of the Liberal party, and government buildings leased from other fat

May 14, 1981
The Economy
cat friends of the Liberal party. They leave their lights on all night for which the taxpayers of Canada must pay. We have unnecessary government advertising on television and in our newspapers which costs the people of this country a tremendous amount in tax dollars. We have an unnecessary proliferation of Crown corporations. Mr. Speaker, those are just a few of the tremendously large number of extravagant and wasteful examples of incompetence and inefficient spending by this government. There is one final example which made me laugh. 1 read that we commissioned an American artist to prepare a design for a Canadian postage stamp commemorating energy. The artist used a U.S. nuclear reactor to depict our Canadian nuclear industry. How ridiculous, and who is in charge? Where is the economic competence in that bunch of bumber-shooting so-and-so's over there? Nowhere is the government's mishandling of this economy more evident than in its mismanagement of the fishing industry. The policies of the government are crippling our fishing industry on both coasts, and there are many who say it will not be able to recover.
I want to illustrate just how these economic policies of the government and the mismanagement by our so-called fishermen's fisheries minister are hurting the fishermen of Canada. The fisheries policy in this country is not a product of a well-thought-out management plan but, rather, a series of haphazard decisions made on a day by day basis in reaction to political pressures from one group or another.
The high interest rate policy of the government is forcing more and more fishermen into bankruptcy. Last June, when we were discussing the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, I was hard pressed to understand how the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) wanted to lend more and more money at preferred interest rates to fishermen when there were not enough fish to be provided for the existing fleet. But at that time, of course, fishermen were a good credit risk and, of course, they were borrowing amounts up to $150,000 at one per cent over prime which meant they could borrow at about 13 per cent.
There are now deficits approaching $.5 billion associated with the capitalization of our fishing fleet. Those moneys now carry an interest charge of some 21 per cent. That is creating a tremendous negative impact upon our fishermen. For example, considering a $100,000 vessel, which is not a large vessel by west coast standards, a fisherman would have to pay some $20,000 or $21,000 interest per year merely to service that debt. To make matters worse, the minister is now forcing fishermen on the west coast to restrict their efforts to catch more and more fish each year.
Unlike other industries in Canada, fishermen cannot increase their effort to compensate for higher expenses. The Fraser River gillnet fleet can attest to this. Many of those fishermen made only a few thousand dollars of take-home pay last year, and the dilemma they face this year, in facing the prospect of losing their homes or their vessels, must be placed
squarely in the lap of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the government's indifferent approach to high interest rates.
As mentioned earlier, this House passed legislation last June which guaranteed a fisherman's loan to a maximum of $150,000 at I per cent over prime. The minister at the time indicated that this program would enable the fishermen to retain their independence so they would not have to look to the big fishing companies for financing. The problem now is that the fishermen cannot obtain financing from the processors because they themselves are in tremendous financial difficulty as a result of the high interest policies of this government. Furthermore, that cheap, chiselling Canadian government is garnisheeing the wages of these fishermen through the fishing companies in order to try to balance their budget when the fishermen are faced with absolute bankruptcy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Just recently I received a letter from a constituent of mine who has been a fisherman on the west coast for many years. In April his bank manager informed him that the interest rate on his fisheries improvement loan would be hiked to 19 per cent. Tomorrow, I suppose it will be 21 per cent. I would like to read an excerpt from that letter. My constituent writes:
Just to give you an example of what we are up against, I just completed two weeks fishing on the west coast during which I was able to get out fishing 3'h days and caught a total of 15 fish worth $308.
He could not even pay for his fuel, let alone the interest on his loan!
I cannot fish the inside waters where we could do considerably better this time of year due to new regulations introduced this year. I don't think that I have to repeat to you our problems which all seem to be coming to a head this year and will no doubt result in financial failure of some fishermen.
That letter is not an isolated instance. I receive letters like that every day in my office. So I did some checking, and a few days ago we called the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to obtain some information on just how many fishermen were defaulting on their fisheries improvement loans. I was told by an official of the department that to date there have been some 237 requests to rewrite the terms of the loan; that means, to refinance at higher interest rates and longer pay-out periods. One hundred and eighty-six of those loans were to British Columbia fishermen. Of those 186 provisions, the departmental official estimated that between 10 per cent and 15 per cent of those loans to 18 or 25 fishermen had already been defaulted. They were faced with foreclosure.
That sounded bad enough, but I decided to check with a number of banks and credit unions in the Vancouver area. From these sources, the situation turned out to be much worse than that depicted by fisheries department officials. According to bank contacts in Vancouver, many loans were in arrears, and not only those under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act; but the banks have decided to carry the fishermen with the hope that the fishing season will improve from last year's disastrous season, and also because fishermen have historically been good credit risks. However, one official indicated to me
May 14, 1981

that 85 per cent of his loan portfolio to fishermen on the west coast could be called in on very, very valid grounds tomorrow if he chose to do so. Another official at the British Columbia Central Credit Union estimated that 25 per cent of the B.C. fleet is now in serious financial trouble. If the 1981 fishing season does not show a drastic improvement, that percentage will increase substantially.
What frightens me and many fishermen is that this season cannot be any better than the last because the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has imposed tough restrictions on the various gear-type fishermen out on the west coast. If this is the case, it is hard to imagine that the banks will continue to extend credit for another year.
The processing industry in this country is not healthy either. For example, one of the largest packing houses in cannery operations in Canada, the B.C. Packers Company, suffered a $14 million loss last year on a capital investment of $200 million. That is a 7 per cent operating loss. At the Fisheries Council of Canada meeting here this week, we learned that the processors are having a difficult time staying in business because in the last two or three years the percentage of the value of fish returned to fishermen has increased from a traditional average of 45 per cent to some 70 per cent. I am not criticizing that. We want to see the fishermen get a greater percentage of the wholesale value of the produced product. But what we have here is the possibility of a compound failure: that fishermen will have their loans called and the companies which will buy their fish will find themselves collapsing as a consequence. I hope I have made my point very clear. This government has to start to move to cut its spending. It is an absolute waste.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Deniger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour and a great pleasure to take part in such a significant debate on the economy. Among other things, the motion introduced by the official opposition party stresses interest rates and the inflation rate. Keeping in mind the short time allotted to me tonight, Mr. Speaker, I will attempt to review the Canadian economic situation as I see it and to suggest five possible and positive solutions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), particularly with a view to lightening the burden of inflation for small wage earners.
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. once wrote that taxes are the price we must pay for a civilized society. Although Mr. Holmes has lost none of his impressive reputation, his principles do appear increasingly less convincing. Indeed, far be it from us to believe that our civilization is worth all that much, particularly in light of the events of these past few days. Mr. Speaker, the interest rates are very high, they have even reached unprecedented levels. Members opposite and government members as well have given us a whole series of examples of the dramatic effects of those soaring interest rates. Mr. The Economy
Speaker, certain members on both sides of the House are even standing on the edge of bankruptcy. In my riding of Laprairie on Montreal's south shore, and that includes the cities of Saint-Lambert, Greenfield Park, LeMoyne, Brossard, Laprairie and Candiac, I went to the trouble of sending a questionnaire to my constituents. Over 5,000 took time out to answer and send me the results. Very telling and very significant they are, those results, because to my first question in which I asked my constituents of Laprairie what they thought was the most important topic-and I listed energy, the economy, constitutional reform, international security and North-South relations-out of those five options 57.3 per cent of respondents picked the economy as being the most pressing subject, whereas among the others energy rallied 14 per cent and constitutional reform 9 per cent. Some 57.3 per cent of the people checked the economy as being their first preoccupation and 20 per cent ranked the economy second among their current concerns. It seems obvious therefore that in my riding just as in the riding of all members, the economy is the subject which draws most interest.
Here is a point I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because certain members opposite keep harping on it. I asked the people of the riding of Laprairie whether they thought that a price freeze is necessary. Forty-nine per cent of them replied that a price freeze is necessary, against 35 per cent who said no. Surprisingly enough, Mr. Speaker, when I asked about a wage freeze the results were the exact opposite-35 per cent told me that a wage freeze is necessary whereas 48 per cent said that it is not. Therefore, that reflects a certain confusion, a certain dichotomy which now prevails among people about the economic situation, precisely because they hear so many things that they are really wondering who is speaking the truth and who is not.
Mr. Speaker, interest rates are setting the price of money and the price of money, like the price of any other goods, has never been so high. But let us not forget that interest rates are not set artificially, but rather by the market pressures every Thursday. Today, once again, people got together and bid on treasury bills, resulting in a given rate of interest. The forces at play in the marketplace, at least to my mind, are the very foundation of free enterprise, the society we so heartily hope for, the society hon. members of the opposition claim we do not represent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this interest rate which is set by the market on a weekly basis has now reached a record high. Of course, opposition members keep reminding us that interest rates are rising, that prices are rising, but they forget a carelessness I am quite willing to overlook to mention that the income of all citizens in the country has grown in the last ten years. Lest I am accused of being insensitive, may I be allowed to remind hon. members, and Canadians who are listening to us, that in the past ten years, prices have increased by 90 per cent while the average income of Canadians has easily exceed-

May 14, 1981
The Economy
ed those prices by 100 per cent. The increase is therefore considerably greater than that of prices, and this means that we are clearly richer now than we were ten years ago. The fact remains, however, that we have a high inflation rate, and high unemployment.
The cost of money, Mr. Speaker, whether we like it or not, is directly related to inflation, and inflation is 12.4 per cent higher this year than a year ago; if interest rates were not at a higher level than the rate of inflation, no one then could afford to lend money. Money then would no longer have any value. Naturally, no more money would be available because the money lent would not yield as much income as could be earned by borrowing it. The whole economy would crumble. It has often been suggested, as a solution, that the interest rates be reduced artificially, in such an economic situation, to a rate lower than the inflation rate; but that strikes me as an absolutely irresponsible solution.
There is, of course, the problem of the American prime rate which has now reached 19.5 per cent. If the Canadian rate were to be substantially and artificially reduced while the American rate remained at its current level, certain major investors would obviously be seriously tempted to invest whatever money they have in the United States to obtain a higher rate of return. We often praise the wisdom of those Canadians who, every fall when the new interest rate on treasury bonds is announced, sell the bonds they then hold if the new rate is higher and purchase new bonds at the higher rate.
Mr. Speaker, I am referring to the small Canadian investor who has $1,000 or $2,000 invested in these types of bonds. If this small investor can make such a decision, it is easy to imagine what a major investor would do. If there were such an outflow of capital, there would obviously be less capital to invest, and this would inevitably bring about a devaluation of the Canadian dollar and an increase in inflation. Of course, those who would benefit from this devaluated Canadian dollar would certainly be the representatives of export companies, but as we know, Mr. Speaker, these companies are already in a privileged situation and they are making more money than ever before now that the dollar has reached a low mark of 83 cents. And, of course, those who would suffer would be all of us, who would have to pay more for the goods that we import.
Mr. Speaker, in the situation that I have described, there lurks, of course, a tragedy, the tragedy which now affects the small wage earners. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the small wage earners are the hardest hit by inflation.
Last April, Mr. Jean Poulin wrote in La Presse that, according to the figures supplied by the Quebec Bureau of Statistics, in that province the purchasing power of those in the higher income brackets was constantly increasing as compared with that of small wage earners.
In 1970, for instance, in the mining sector, the average salary was $149.80. In 1980, this salary had gone up to $446.80, a jump of 198 per cent, from which we must subtract
a general price increase of 92 per cent, and this gives an actual increase in purchasing power of 106 per cent. This is quite good for the mining sector, which has, of course, known an upsurge. In the business sector, the average salary has increased from $101.68 to $244.70, for an increase of 141 per cent. When the 92 per cent for price increases is subtracted, an actual increase in purchasing power of 49 per cent is obtained.
In the services sector, wages have increased from $91 to $225, or by 145 per cent, minus the price increase of 92 per cent, which gives an actual increase of 53 per cent, and I shall pass by other sectors such as finance, manufacturing, transportation and construction, and simply note that those who suffer the most from inflation are the small wage earners because the gap between high and low wages is constantly increasing.
The unfortunate fact which we must try to correct is the impact of inflation on small wage earners who are the hardest hit by any increase in housing and food costs. A person whose earnings exceed $25,000 may more easily face cost of living increases than a person whose earnings fall between $10,000 and $15,000. I have now come to the point in my speech, Mr. Speaker, where I intend to suggest to the minister tangible and positive action to reduce inflation without penalizing the small wage earners.
Mr. Speaker, first we should stop granting salary increases on a percentage basis; second, we should have a new cost of living index based on the margin between the bare necessities of the small wage earner which take up most of those increases and such necessities obviously include transportation, accommodation and food. Let me dwell on those two suggestions. When I talk about salary increases granted not on a percentage basis but on the basis of a certain amount of money, this is what I mean.
If the total increase in the price of those essential items amounted, let us say, to $1,789 in 1981, it would be utterly unrealistic for a Canadian worker to obtain any salary increase short of the minimum amount actually representing the increase in his cost of living because it is clear that if you earn $40,000 and get a 10 per cent increase, the impact will not be the same as if you earned $10,000 and also got a 10 per cent increase, even though in both cases the same percentage is allowed. It is ridiculous. Mr. Speaker, that the small wage earner who is more severely affected by inflation should get a 10 per cent increase, just like the well-paid worker who has plenty of everything. Mr. Speaker, how could we realistically expect to reduce the gap between the haves and the have-nots in this country unless we develop a new formula for granting wage increases. It is not only the small wage earner who should get that through their heads, but also the unions, the unionized workers, the hon. members of this House, the professionals and a great many others.
Concerning the new cost of living index which I have also suggested, I do not think that including as we do now in the index the costs of luxury items such as new cars and houses
May 14, 1981

makes any sense. It seems to me that they do not represent everyday expenses. It is clear that the price index is altogether erratic and does not really reflect the facts of life. In other words, Mr. Speaker, wage increases should be granted on a dollar basis and not on a percentage basis, and should be tied to the price increase of essential goods and services. The wage increases would therefore be in line with the price increases of our everyday needs.
The haves, the well-to-do, the rich, the higher-income groups would then have to bear the burden of inflation by paying themselves for the higher cost of goods which, I suggest, they are so to speak the only ones to consume, because the small wage earner cannot afford a new car or a new home, Mr. Speaker. When one compares the standard of living of the low-income groups, the have-nots with that of the haves, Mr. Speaker, one finds an absurd and nonsensical situation.
Such anomalies should be corrected once and for all because it is obvious that under that formula, a 10 per cent increase on a $40,000 salary is twice more inflationary than a 10 per cent hike on a $10,000 salary, and this requires, obviously, a new approach in our labour relations, a new method of having a dialogue between labour and management. But if there is no willingness to make new overtures, we will get nowhere in our society.
A third solution, Mr. Speaker, that I want to bring to the attention of the House has to do with a report on regulatory reform on which I had the opportunity of working. The task force was made up, of course, of both opposition and government members and last December we tabled our findings pursuant to our terms of reference. After several months of hearings, I came to the conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that the people who watch us in this House believe that the size of the government must be reduced and that competition among businesses must be encouraged further.
Mr. Speaker, this is exactly what our report deals with, and in my view this unfortunately has not yet been desired by the government, at least to my satisfaction. After numerous hearings we produced a report in which we submitted some 57 recommendations. We urged the minister to give very careful consideration to these 57 recommendations. He gave that commitment, but we have yet to see the results. Although usually patient, I am more and more anxious that the minister give a positive answer to the 57 recommendations in that report. Other solutions, on which unfortunately I cannot dwell this evening for lack of time, deal with something essential in my view, the reduction of bureaucracy in this country and a formal commitment to increase competition and productivity.
I do not share the view that all of our Crown corporations should be sold. But this is a far cry from getting involved into every economic sector. Unfortunately, and I say this in all frankness, often when the government got involved in some particular segment, that segment experienced a slowdown in activity, productivity declined in some cases, and competition
The Economy
suffered because governments have resources that small businesses do not have.
Mr. Speaker, I have proposed this evening five measures that are essential in my view if we are once and for all to tackle positively the problems of inflation. To conclude, let me remind hon. members and all those who are listening today that Canada has no other choice but to fight inflation. Where differences may arise is on the ways of doing this. Hon. members opposite offered some suggestions and we offered others. I for one suggested ways to fight inflation especially as it affects the poorer Canadians, those who are without means as compared to those who are in better financial circumstances. I especially stated the case of the poorer elements of our society because they are the hardest hit by inflation.
Mr. Speaker, I avoided tonight the short-term measures which unfortunately are often proposed in this House by politicians who are more inclined to put forward politically acceptable rather than economically acceptable solutions. There is no easy answer to this problem and the situation will only get worse unless we are prepared today to make the necessary sacrifices. If the Minister of Finance was here tonight I would say to him: Mr. Minister, I would not want your job for anything in the world. But you are doing a great job and you have my support all the way.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who preceded me mentioned that if the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) were here, he would make certain remarks. I am sad that he is not here because I would not tell him that he is doing a good job. Interest rates are running at 20 per cent. We have massive government deficits and massive balance of payments problems. I do not see how anyone in his right mind could tell the Minister of Finance that he is doing a good job. I do not see how any Canadian, whether he be a businessman, engaged in farming or running a household, could tell that minister he is doing a good job. That is one of the problems we have with the economy today.
I spent some time in my riding during the past two or three weeks. I had a chance to talk to the people who make this country productive, those who meet the payrolls and talk to their bankers on a regular basis. A feeling of almost helplessness pervades many of those I spoke to. They have the feeling that nobody knows what they are doing. It is incumbent that all of us stay away from the rhetoric of which the chairman of the finance committee spoke here this afternoon and make some real suggestions to the government to help with this situation.
Many people are very unhappy with what they hear from the economists. It makes one think that nobody understands what is going on in the economy. That is the problem with economists, there are too many fuzzy thinkers today.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
This reminds me of a story, and if I can have your indulgence I will relate it very briefly. This story involves a man who bought a hot air balloon. I think hot air is something that should not be unfamiliar to this chamber. On a Sunday afternoon, this man decided he was going to fly his balloon. He got a friend to go with him. They got out in the country and found a field from which they could fly their balloon. They got it up and got going. During the heat of the day, some clouds developed. They got into the clouds and could not see the ground. They became very concerned about how they were going to manage this balloon. All of a sudden they drifted into a clearing and there was a man down in a field below them. They hollered down to this man: "Where are we?" The man heard them, looked up at the balloon and said: "You are in a balloon". Just then the two balloonists drifted off into the clouds and they could not talk to the man on the ground. The one friend said to the other: "That looked like an economist to me". The other man said: "Why would that look like an economist? I thought it was a farmer out in his field." His friend said: "Who else could give us such accurate, precise and utterly useless information except an economist?"
I think this is what is happening to our economy. Everybody talks about 20 per cent interest rates, they talk about big balance of payments deficits and they talk about billions of dollars that nobody can comprehend. Yet nobody does anything, or appears to be able to do anything, about our economic problems. This is a very sad situation. I think an admonition can be directed in this respect at the Bank of Canada.
We saw the present Governor of the Bank of Canada at the helm of that institution in the 1973-74 period when the money supply increased at the rate of as much as 20 per cent for no apparent reason. I should not say it was for no apparent reason because it was to help finance increased government deficits created by members opposite who then formed the government. We saw the Bank of Canada maintain our dollar at a premium in the 1976-77 period when we had, for no structural or productive reason, a dollar that was overvalued. They kept the value of the dollar high simply by raising interest rates artificially.
I would argue very strongly that we are making a mistake now by using interest rates to regulate the value of our dollar externally. I do not know who decides on this magic figure of 82 cents, 83 cents or 84 cents for our Canadian dollar, but clearly that is what is going on at the weekly auctions every Thursday that take place at the Bank of Canada. We witnessed it today when, for the first time that I am aware of, 90-day treasury bills yielded the same as 180-day treasury bills, that is, 18.73 per cent. Normally there is quite a spread between the close on 90-day bills and the 180-day bills. This indicates there was massive intervention by the Bank of Canada today in that auction.
To my mind that is certainly not a floating interest rate. It is an interest rate that is regulated in terms of keeping the value of the Canadian dollar at a certain level. There are many of us who would sooner see, if that is an option, and I think it is a
real option to some degree, a lower Canadian dollar and, as a result, a lower interest rate. If what I hear from some bankers and some economists is right, when they say they think our dollar is undervalued, there should be no concern about honestly letting the dollar float.
In fact, the real value of the dollar is determined by our international dealings and the demand for our dollars as a result of the ability of our Canadian dollar to buy what Canadians produce. If in fact our Canadian economy is only as productive as a 75-cent dollar, an 80-cent dollar or a 90-cent dollar would indicate, it would seem to me that should be the proper way to determine the value of the Canadian dollar. Let it honestly be determined on the marketplace. To do otherwise is to kid ourselves.
I argued this point in 1976-77 when we kept our dollar artificially at a higher level than it should have been for structural and productive reasons. When the crunch came, we saw the value of our dollar fall lower than it needed to. I believe very strongly that we are making that same kind of mistake today.
The Minister of Finance said in the House yesterday in the course of debate, as reported at page 9532 of Hansard:
If, in the course of debate today and tomorrow, hon. members can bring forward some new, alternative ideas that, because of their validity, would demand immediate implementation, then I would consider doing that very thing.
I would point out to him that many of us in this House have moved motions under Standing Order 43 to refer the very serious interest rate question to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I will read into the record again a motion I had the opportunity to propose on Wednesday, April 22, which appears at page 9383 of Hansard. This motion has exactly the same wording as a motion which we accepted when we were the government. It was moved by the now Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) in October, 1979. If the Minister of Finance is really serious about finding some solutions to high interest rates, I would challenge him to accept the reference to the finance committee that we accepted when we were in government.
The motion is as follows:
That this House immediately order its Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to undertake an immediate review of the interest rate policy of this government and the Bank of Canada, and that for this purpose the governor of the bank and the Minister of Finance appear before it to explain their actions and what they will be doing to solve the problems which the governor of the bank himself said, regarding interest rates, are now being caused for individuals and business.
As I said, a similar motion was accepted by our government back in October 1979 when interest rates were in the range of 13 per cent or 14 per cent. Today interest rates are at 20 per cent. If there was an urgency about the matter then, which we as the government found legitimate, certainly that urgency is all the more legitimate now when we see interest rates at the astronomical figure of 20 per cent.
When one sees the Bank of Canada setting bank interest rates at 18.98 per cent it makes one think that very soon we are going to have prime rates in this country at 20 per cent. Most lines of credit for prime borrowers from the bank who
May 14, 1981

operate under this kind of a floating rate, have their interest rates calculated monthly, so that on an annual basis they are operating with an interest rate at over 20 per cent. To me this is an astronomical, a killer figure as far as keeping our economy productive is concerned.
I know 20 minutes is not a long time but I would like very briefly, if I may, to relate some of my remarks to agriculture and the way that industry needs to use credit, and to conclude by offering what I think are some positive suggestions to the government that do not imply or indicate increased government spending.
Briefly, agriculture is a very large user of credit. Not only is it a large user of credit, it is a very important sector of the Canadian economy. It is important, I would argue, for three reasons. A productive agricultural economy is the foundation of any developed country. I am proud to point out again, and proud to be part of the agricultural industry, that Canadian consumers spend as small a percentage of their take-home pay on food as consumers in any other country in the world. We in this country are privileged to be able to feed ourselves on something like 18 per cent of our disposable income. This is on an average; I am not talking about many people who are unfortunately unable to get by on their earnings and spend less than 18 per cent on food. On the average, 18 per cent of our take-home pay is spent on food. That means that over 80 per cent can be spent on other things such as colour TV, paid vacations, and still be able to enjoy short work weeks and many other things we take for granted in this country.
In order to accomplish that, the Canadian agricultural industry over the years has had to become very, very productive. In fact, as an industry it has increased its productivity more than any other sector of our economy. As I said, 1 am proud to be associated with an industry which has that kind of a record.
In addition, over the last number of years not only have we in agriculture been able to lower the amount of the disposable income Canadians spend on food, we have also, at the same time, been able to increase our exports. We as the Canadian agricultural industry, even though we import something like $5 billion worth of food, still export close to $9 billion worth of food. Having regard to the surplus in the balance of payments, the Canadian agricultural industry is responsible for large foreign earnings. This is very important to the Canadian dollar, because as we earn more Canadian dollars, there is less pressure on our Canadian dollar and this helps hold the value of the Canadian dollar at a higher level, and therefore allows the government to get by with lower interest rates.
It seems to me that if the government were serious in some of its long-range economic plans, it should be encouraging this very important part of our Canadian economy, the agricultural industry, to increase its capacity to produce and increase our exports of agricultural products. In the process of doing this, we will be lowering the amount of the disposable income we spend on food, we will also be increasing our foreign earnings and thereby alleviating the serious situation in which we find ourselves today.
The Economy
I also think we have an obligation to the rest of the world. We as Canadians have under our control something like five times more arable land per citizen than any other country in the world.
We have an obligation in that regard to see that we make use of this land as best we can because, as we all know, we as a global entity are not expanding our food production as fast as the world population is growing.
In terms of the Canadian economy, some 10 per cent of our gross national product is produced by the agricultural industry. One out of four, or 25 per cent of the labour force, is involved in some way or another in the agrifood sector of Canada. This gives us an idea of how important agriculture is, not only to the agricultural community but also to the whole economy.
I would like to talk specifically for a minute about the Canadian beef industry. Many of us have come to rely on beef as a staple in our diets. In fact, on average 2.5 per cent of consumer spending is on beef. The beef industry in Canada is a very large user of credit. It has been stated many times before that as interest rates fluctuate on a daily, weekly or monthly basis, the beef industry in Canada is certainly not able to adjust to higher and changing interest rates.
Very briefly, much of the crop which is in the ground now in many parts of the country is being sown with the idea that it should be consumed by livestock. That means that much of the crop which is being sown will not be marketed for a year or even longer. It might not be marketed through livestock for as long as 15 months. When interest rates change, as they have in the past two or three years, producers simply cannot adjust to short-term interest rate changes. It is the planting season in our country and many producers are now in the process of committing themselves to a year or a year and a half production period, and they are committing themselves not to market much of the crop which is going in the ground now until the summer of 1982. They cannot adjust to short-term interest rates. This is a very large problem for many producers.
A feedlot of 500 or 600 head is not a particularly large feedlot, but it could be considered to be of a size sufficient to be a family operation. Many operators of feedlots of this size are now paying as much as $100 in interest a day. Farmers are met with many uncertainties. They meet uncertainties with respect to weather conditions, rainfall, hail, disease and many other things, but most farmers would agree that the biggest uncertainty they face is government decisions. One of the government decisions over which producers have no control whatsoever is with respect to what interest rates will be. Rather than go through that kind of uncertainty, this year many farmers will choose not to produce at all. With interest rates at the 20 per cent level, one cannot do very much but agree with them. That is one of the very real problems we have now.
The Governor of the Bank of Canada has said many times that monetary policy, or raising or lowering interest rates, and

May 14, 1981
The Economy
regulating the supply of money is only one factor in fighting inflation. He is fighting it from the demand side by trying to slow down the rate at which people borrow and thereby slow down the inflationary expectations people in this country have. But when we have a 20 per cent interest rate, I argue very strongly that that hurts more on the supply side than it helps on the demand side because, as the example I have just given illustrates, an interest rate of 20 per cent chases people out of the beef industry and thereby puts less beef on the consumer's plate over the next year or year and a half. That will drive prices up drastically because there will not be as much beef available. The supposed cure we are being fed by this government and the Bank of Canada, namely, high interest rates, will actually do more damage on the supply side and thereby make inflation worse. This is something the government fails to realize. That is why many people are becoming very sick and tired of some of the fuzzy ideas and statistics we are being fed. It is time many of us took a look at the real situation in the real world. The real situation is not found in this chamber, and certainly not in offices where paper is shuffled. The real world is out where the real production goes on in this country.
I will give the House another example. Many people have pointed out that in the northern hemisphere we have six months of winter and six months to get ready for it. In many areas of this country that means when you raise cows, you spend half of the year feeding them. That is a direct cost. When interest rates are at 20 per cent, by far the biggest cost of maintaining a cow in western Canada is the interest cost. That cost is greater than the cost of feeding that animal for six months of the year.
We find ourselves in an absolutely ludicrous position. Let us not kid ourselves into thinking that high interest rates will help reduce inflation, when actually they are driving out the very basic business we need in this country, and that is food production.
To quote some figures, last year Canadian farmers paid some $1.5 billion in interest. This year the estimate is that they could pay as much as $2 billion in interest. That is an increase of roughly one third over last year's interest costs. We all know that last year's interest costs were very high. According to the figures I have here, the cost of money has increased two and a half times faster than the cost of any other commodity with which a farmer has to work. It is one factor to have that cost go up, but to have it go up, not to be able to calculate it in terms of budgeting and to have it increase in an unpredictable fashion is even worse. As I said previously, the biggest variable with which any of us in the agricultural community work is the variable which is associated with government because there really is no rhyme or reason for some of the things governments do.
I have five suggestions to make to the government. If the Minister of Finance is serious about what he said yesterday in question period, I challenge him to take some of the suggestions I am about to make extremely seriously. My first suggestion is to make the small business development bond available to unincorporated businesses and to make it available for
purposes other than the very limited capital items for which it is now available. I will elaborate on that, if I might. As we all know, the small business development bond has limitations to it. It is limited to $500,000. You can only have it once, and it is limited now to incorporated businesses. Its rate is set over a period of five years. It is a fixed rate, and it is set at half the prime rate plus whatever one can negotiate with the bank, usually between 1 per cent and 2 per cent. At present, if we have a 20 per cent prime rate and if we take half of that, that would be 10 per cent. If we added, let us say, 1.5 per cent, we would be looking at 11.5 per cent as opposed to 20 per cent. That certainly is a very significant reduction in the interest rate. The beauty of this small business development bond concept to me is, first, that administratively we do not create a large bureaucracy. All we have is a very small number of people over in the Department of Finance approving these bonds as they come in. They look at them to see that they fit the categories defined-

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate the indulgence of the House. I did not realize my time went so quickly.
To put it briefly, the small business development bond should be "liberalized," if I can use that word. I think everyone opposite would agree with that.
Second, the Canadian Wheat Board initial payments should be set as high as possible. The Canadian Wheat Board is able to borrow at prime minus one-quarter per cent. When we have high interest rates, cash flow becomes almost as important as price. The government should encourage the Canadian Wheat Board to set initial payments as high as possible. The minister currently responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board decided
May 14, 1981

not to announce initial prices until after seeding is completed. I think that was a mistake.
Third, the Agricultural Stabilization Act is the law of the land. We all know that there will be a pay-out to hog producers this year. That pay-out should be made as quickly as possible. Can hon. members believe that we are a year behind in some of those payments? If use of the Agricultural Stabilization Act could be made with respect to the hog industry, or whatever industry it is to apply to this year, as quickly as possible, that would assist producers significantly with their cash flows.
Fourth, I suggest we have fixed financing for livestock and other farming operations so that a person who has to feed cattle for six months or a year could go into a bank and instead of having his loan rate float, he could fix his interest rate for the productive period of that enterprise, just as is done now for a house mortgage.
There should also be some other way of rationing credit. For instance, at the moment I can get a loan to go to Florida cheaper than I can get a loan to buy a tractor. That is not right. It is a misuse of credit.
Finally, in my opinion, the structure of the Bank of Canada should be changed to have at least two elected members from this House sitting on the bank's board of directors. The Bank of Canada has more to do with fiscal policy than we think it has. That is the basis of our whole parliamentary system to have elected members oversee fiscal affairs. I would argue very strongly that having elected members on the board of directors of the Bank of Canada would be very beneficial to us in the long run.
I thank the House again for its indulgence in allowing me some extra time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very happy to relinquish some time to the hon. member for Portage-Marquette so that his recommendations could be put on the record. I can assure him that I will look at them very carefully and so will the minister.
Yesterday I spoke on the motion specifically dealing with interest rates and I tried to deal with the fundamental factors that were underlying the current level of interest rates, why interest rates are where they are and what factors determine interest rates.
Tonight I want to expand into the relationship between interest rates, the economy and economic growth and what the government has done about these things. Today we have heard some criticism of the government's economic policy. Some members from the opposition indicated that the federal government has no consistent economic policy. That is simply not correct. The federal government does have an economic policy which is consistent and, given the appropriate time taken for economic policy to take effect, the government's policy will be effective. It will yield the kinds of results that we all want to have, which are lower unemployment, higher economic
The Economy
growth, greater job creation, going along with lower unemployment, lower rates of inflation and thereby lower rates of interest.
The government's economic policy has three basic thrusts to it. These were laid out in the budget speech which was presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). The first major thrust of the government's budgetary and economic policy was to restrain government spending. Hon. members opposite may say that was not a serious proposition put forward by the Minister of Finance, but it was a very serious proposition. In fact, we have done better than was forecast in the budget of last October.
The second major thrust of the budget and the government's policy is the reordering of the government's priorities in expenditures toward greater expenditures in the areas of economic development, industrial readjustment and job creation. There have been a number of programs introduced in the area of job creation by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). The other day, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) laid out in his speech a very comprehensive framework within which he will be constructing, along with the rest of the cabinet, his industrial policy for Canada. There is a great amount of hope in that framework because it is very comprehensive and one which promises to be workable and to move Canada in the direction we all want it to move. Specifically, Canada has greater manufacturing capability, more growth and more job creation in areas that will enable Canada to have a real economic and industrial future.
The final thrust of the government's economic and budgetary policy is the thrust toward reducing the rate of inflation through a monetary policy which deals with the fundamentals giving rise to inflation.
We have heard members of the official opposition and members of the New Democratic Party calling for a new budget not only today but previously. But let us look at the facts. Let us look at the situation which has arisen subsequent to last October's budget. When I spoke during the budget debate, I spoke strongly in support of the Minister of Finance. Events, I think, will prove that we were right in supporting the Minister of Finance in that budget because it was a good budget and it is working.
Since last October what have we seen? Take the fourth quarter of 1980, at the beginning of which the budget was introduced. In that fourth quarter and in the remaining 19801981 fiscal year, the minister forecast growth rates in the economy and he forecast unemployment rates. The minister talked about job creation and housing starts as well. All of those things outlined in the budget were relatively pessimistic. The outlook was not the way we would have liked to have seen it. But everything was presented very forthrightly in the budget by the Minister of Finance. What has happened subsequently? The events which have transpired since then have laid bare the criticism of the opposition. This criticism still arises today, even flying in the face of what has happened over the last six months in Canada. I ask again, what have we seen over the last six months?

May 14, 1981
The Economy
In the fourth quarter of 1980 we had an annualized growth rate of 8 per cent. In the first quarter of 1981, we have an annualized growth rate, because the figures are not yet finalized, of between 4 per cent and 6 per cent. Those are very high growth rates by Canadian standards, and they are very high growth rates by world standards. In other words, we have had a very strong record of economic growth in the last six months, much above what was forecast in the budget of October 28.
Let me ask what has happened with regard to unemployment. The Minister of Finance put forward a pessimistic outlook with regard to employment. But instead, as the minister pointed out, for the month of April we had the lowest unemployment rate we have had in the last five years. We have a seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of 7 per cent. What did the budget forecast? It forecast unemployment to be over 8 per cent. Therefore, we have done much better than what was forecast in the budget, both in economic growth and in the area of unemployment. Part of that is as a result of how much better we have done in the area of job creation than the budget forecast. As both the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the Minister of Finance mentioned, we have created 346,000 jobs in the last twelve months. We have seen employment in Canada grow by 3.3 per cent. That is the highest rate of growth of employment of any country in the industrialized world bar none. In the area of job creation, Canada has consistently had the highest rate of job growth over the last ten years. That pattern is continuing. The government is committed to creating jobs and to giving opportunities to Canadians. It is committed to providing the kind of environment in which the private sector can create opportunities for Canadians as well. The proof is right there in the facts, not in the rhetoric of the opposition but in the facts. The facts are there.
Let us look at housing starts. We do have a situation in Canada in which lower-income Canadians are having difficulty if they wish to buy a house. But to say that the housing market is in a shambles is not facing the facts. Housing starts are well above 240,000 units a year, which is in the upper range of what Canadians have historically experienced in past years. The housing market, as far as new construction is concerned, is picking up. It is booming.
We could go on and on and look at statistics in other areas. I would like to focus on the budget itself and on the government's commitment to fiscal restraint, to restraint of government expenditure and to a reduction of the deficit and financial requirements. Today the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) and other opposition members told us that in fact government spending is out of control, that the deficit and financial requirements are out of control, and that the government is putting excessive pressures on the financial markets. If we look at the budget figures and what was projected in it, we will see that a reduction was projected in the rate of growth of federal government expenditures. Also there was projected a reduction over time of the deficit and, of course, a reduction in financial requirements which is the amount the federal government must borrow in capital markets.
The facts are that we have done appreciably better than what was forecast in the budget. We have not done worse, we have done better. In fiscal year 1980-81 which just finished, expenditures are $300 million less than were forecast in the budget. The budget deficit has been reduced by over $1.4 billion which is below what was forecast in the budget. The financial requirements in 1980-81 were $1.8 billion less than forecast in the budget.

speechtext:
I hear the hon. member opposite. In fact, when the budget was introduced, we heard from hon. members opposite that the federal government was fooling people, that the estimates were low and were not realistic. They suggested that we would do far worse than was projected, that those were illusory numbers and far below what the government would achieve. In fact, we have done appreciably better than what we forecast in the budget, yet they were called unrealistic numbers by members of the opposition. This clearly indicates the commitment of the Minister of Finance and the government to the two major thrusts which I indicated regarding the budget: restraining government spending and reordering priorities in the government toward economic development, growth, job creation and industrial adjustment. The commitment is there. The programs are coming forward. The job will be done, and it will be done with fiscal responsibility.
In the last two days most of the attention has been focused on the area of interest rates. Sometimes it is very difficult for individual members of Parliament, who deal with very real and pressing problems of constituents, to see beyond those individual problems to the broader macroproblem. I am referring to the problem of how to reorder the economic situation to make the over-all economic situation better for all Canadians. As is often the case, the way to solve the problem for all Canadians is not by trying to solve the problems of every individual Canadian. In some cases we must try to see the forest as well as the trees. This is the case with regard to inflation.
Today the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) indicated that the way to solve our problem was to bring in expenditure programs to subsidize Canadians who were being adversely affected by high interest rates. All Canadians who borrow, irrespective of whether they are farmers, fishermen, foresters, small businessmen, home owners, or consumers who may want to buy, for example, new cars to drive to work, are adversely affected by high interest rates. Should we bring in a special program to assist one group? For example, if we are to bring in a program to assist farmers, why would we bring in a special expenditure program to assist them in coping with the very real difficulties they face with high interest rates and not do the same thing for fishermen, home owners or small businessmen?
Today the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition suggested a program to introduce a mortgage interest and property tax credit. If we look at the 1979 budget of the hon. member for
May 14, 1981

St, John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and ask ourselves how much that program would cost annually when fully implemented, we would be looking at a program which would cost over $2.5 billion per year. If we talk about an energy tax credit, we are talking about half a billion dollars to $1 billion per year. If we brought in an expenditure program to assist all groups which have, justifiably, been identified by hon. members opposite as well as by members on this side of the House, and we say that all of these groups affected by the present high interest rate situation should be subsidized by the federal government, we would find that the only way to do it would be to give way on the expenditure restraint, on the commitment to reduce the deficit, and on the commitment to bring inflation under control. If we give way on the fight against inflation, we will not have lower interest rates; they will be higher. Inflation causes interest rates to be what they are; it is not the other way around. If inflation is at 13 per cent or 14 per cent, the interest rates will be 18 per cent or 19 per cent. If the inflation rate is 20 per cent or 22 per cent, the interest rates will be 25 per cent to 27 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Obviously I am speaking the truth and it is hurting hon. members of the opposition because they are coming alive. In fact, the official whip of the opposition has never been more animated for a man of his size; it is quite something.
As I indicated last night, the prime factor in the interest rates we face today is the rate of inflation. It is the prime determining factor of interest rates. The second factor is the transition phase through which we are going in bringing inflation under control. It involves a reduction in the growth rate in the money supply. If the Bank of Canada reduces the growth rate in the money supply, it means the real funds available for borrowing in capital markets are reduced, but at the same time we are facing increasing demands on capital
The Economy
markets for lending funds. So there is an increasing demand for credit at the same time as we are trying to restrain the supply of available funds in order to bring inflation under control. This is causing pressure on interest rates. Also, as I mentioned last night, the last factor is the high rates in the United States which lead to cash flows in and out of Canada as interest rates fluctuate. If our rates drop significantly below the United States rates, funds will flow out. This will mean lower amounts of lending funds in Canada, which means the supply of funds will diminish and, for a given demand, interest rates will go up or the dollar will drop. Some hon. members have said that we should let the dollar drop. We import at the present time 25 per cent to 30 per cent of our gross national product. If we allow the dollar to drop dramatically from its current level, and if we are really concerned about inflation, we should think about the impact of a dramatic drop in the value of the dollar on the inflation rate when 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the cost of what we import immediately rises by exactly the amount of the drop in the dollar. We are talking about food and energy. We are talking about manufactured products and about a great many services and goods which Canadians buy every day in the marketplace. That is not a solution because by dropping the dollar you immediately feed inflation. When you feed inflation, you do not lead the country to lower interest rates. In fact, you lead the country to higher interest rates in the short term. We cannot allow a declining dollar policy. We cannot let inflation go. We cannot follow expenditure programs which will be inflationary and which will lead to increased government expenditures, because that will be inflationary. Inflationary policies like that will not lead to lower interest rates. They will lead to higher interest rates in the very near future. The best solution to our problem is the government policy which is firmly set to do three things: reduce inflation, reduce government deficits in the growth of expenditures and reflect government spending and-
