speechtext: Marvellous.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
I returned from Hamilton on the weekend and I wish to share with the parliamentary secretary something which might just dampen his enthusiasm ever so slightly. I had discussions with a number of young families who at the end of this month will not be able to renew their mortgages. I say to the parliamentary secretary that all of your statistics and all of your grand pronouncements pale into insignificance when you look at the effect of this government's policies on people who go out every day and work for a living, who at the end of the year find that the wages they earn have not kept pace with the cost of living. They find that the wages they worked so hard to

May 14, 1981
The Economy
earn do not allow them to refinance the house they purchased five years ago. I want to put this to the parliamentary secretary: Statistics be damned! I am sick and tired of hearing government members talking about the statistical benefits which flow from this policy which is being pursued, and which is creating great hardships for so many Canadians in every part of this country in almost every walk of life. I find it extremely difficult to contain the anger I feel when 1 look around the country and when I speak to the people whom each of us in this House supposedly represents. I find that these people are being put into difficult financial positions and that the government shrugs and says "Well, statistics tell us that things are better; we can look forward to happy days." I expect the band to strike up "Happy Days are Here Again" any moment.
Fortunately, or unfortunately, there are those of us who take a look not only at what is written down in a statistical sense but who look at the impact of what has happened. When I was preparing my comments for this evening, I thought I would take a moment to review some of the comments which have been made by other members of the house of Commons in other days about the events of the day. I will take but a moment to do that because I think it is important. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I find this whole debate frustrating. I find it frustrating because on either side of the House- and I am sure the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald) will forgive me for saying this-I hear a great deal being said. But when I look at the record of events which have taken place over the course of the last few years I can juxtapose the two. I can put the official opposition back in government and the government back in the official opposition. I can hear exactly the same statements being made. A year ago, on October 26, 1979, the headlines read "High rates 'crucifying' Crosbie concedes". Another headline read "Cros-bie backs interest hike". Another said "Will keep interest up to beat inflation: PCs". There is another unbelievable one which reads: "We live in tough times: Crosbie". Another reads "Time to tough it out Tories warn Canada as inflation mounts". I think to myself, is it not strange, there they were in government saying exactly the same things that the government of today is saying about the conditions which exist today. I will give the Conservatives credit, things were not as bad then as they are now. Things were not as bad for the people of Canada at that time as they are now.
The interesting thing is that while the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and others were saying these things on the other side of the House, when the government was in opposition, we had the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), who is now Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, saying:
-in view of the professed desire of the government to see domestic oil prices rise quickly to world levels, are not the acting minister and his government in fact telling the Canadian people that their policy is to have this country move into a recession?
He then goes on to say:
How can the government continue to justify supporting a policy of following American interest rates so closely, to what are record levels in Canada, when the
soundness of the basis of the American policy has been called into question by U.S. experts? Why does the government not act now to prevent our economy from becoming another Three-Mile Island?
There he was in all his splendour in opposition yapping and yipping about what was going on. Then he gets put into government, and what happens? Things get worse.
Then there was the then leader of the opposition, who is now Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), suggesting that the prime minister of the day, the hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was accepting the record high interest rates without doing anything about it. We saw the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) first quoting the then minister of finance saying:
These people are being crucified with an 11 Zi per cent mortgage rate-
Those are the words of the then minister of finance. Last week they were being crucified with an 18 per cent mortgage rate. At the time of the 11 xh per cent mortgage rate, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) said:
Would the minister make the judgment now that, as a result of his policies and his government's policies we have the mortgage rate going up to 14'/2 per cent, the people of Canada are not being crucified but are being drawn and quartered-
Where is the consistency? I could go on and on. It is embarrassing to read these items. I am surprised that members on both sides are not offended and quitting en masse over the positions which they have put forward in the House over the course of the last two years. Then the government has the nerve to get up and tell us, through the parliamentary secretary, that things are getting better.
Let us take a look at how good things are for a moment. I do not know whether the statistics are new or, for that matter, of any interest, because I doubt very much if anything much will happen in the next year. However, let me tell you that the consumer price index has gone up, since March of 1977, by 37.4 per cent. The automobile price index has gone up by 49.1 per cent in the same period. The gasoline prices in Canada have gone up by 75.4 per cent. The prime rate has gone up 140 per cent plus between 1977 and 1981.
It is interesting to note, though, that not everyone was suffering while this was going on because, of course, the profits of the five major banks went up 76 per cent from 1977 to 1980. That was while all of these very high and onerous costs were being borne by the Canadian public. The assets of the five major banks went up by 96 per cent from 1977 through 1980. While that was going on, bankruptcies rose in Canada between 1977 and 1980 by 65 per cent. So on the one hand we are getting higher and higher costs, and on the other hand we are getting wages which are not keeping pace with the inflation level and are falling behind by 1 per cent or 2 per cent a year. The banks are making ever increasing profit margins. People in business and private individuals across this country are losing their businesses and their homes, and yet we are told that things are getting better.
May 14, 1981

From March of 1980 to March of 1981 bankruptcies in this country have gone up by 29 per cent, and this government sits and twiddles its thumbs and tells us that good things are about to happen. What about those people who have already lost? Who speaks for them? What about the families which cannot find homes to live in because they cannot afford to pay the cost? Who speaks for them? How do we compensate them when things get better? what do we say to them when they have lost $10,000 which they have saved over the course of many years because they could not meet the onerous and usurious rates being charged by the banks? Do we go and apologize, send them a get well card or a sympathy card perhaps? Do we tell them that we are really sorry we did not do anything about it, that it is unfortunate and it is just one of the facts of life? "The statistics are good, so do not feel badly about it. The fact that you have lost everything, we cannot do anything about that." We are just going to sit back and hope that somehow, by some magical, mystical means, inaction will resolve the problem. I do not think inaction can resolve the problem. I have said many times in this House that we have reached a critical point for many Canadian families. We reached it, in fact, about a year ago.
As my leader said yesterday and again today, there are more than a thousand families in Canada which at the end of this month will have to walk away from their homes because they cannot refinance them at the current interest rates. No one can tell me that it is impossible for us in the House of Commons to do something about a situation which has been allowed to occur over the course of successive Liberal and Tory governments since 1975. No one can tell me that it is impossible for us to find a way to bring interest rates down to a level-at least for those home owners who are faced with exorbitant rates today-which can be managed within the income levels of the majority of people. No one can tell me that we must simply sit back and watch while people are left to their own devices, while people walk away and leave their homes or lose their businesses and, perhaps, in the process, lose their homes because they have to go out and mortgage them to keep their businesses going, at a time when the Royal Bank increased its profits between 1977 and 1980 by 94 per cent.
No one can tell me that it is reasonable and fair that the farmer who can no longer make enough money to pay the mortgage will have to leave his farm and go bankrupt, at a time when the Bank of Montreal increased its profits between 1977 to 1980 by 115 per cent. No one can tell me that it is a reasonable thing. We should take a look at the people in this country who are struggling to maintain an economy which is being allowed to be undermined by outside influences, people who cannot get wages which will keep pace with the cost of living. No one can tell me that such a situation is reasonable while the Bank of Nova Scotia has increased its profits between 1977 and 1980 by almost 69 per cent. No one can tell me that the manager of the Toronto-Dominion Bank should have reason to expect an increase of 82 per cent in profits at the same time as he looks families straight in the eye in his
The Economy
office and says, "We cannot renew your mortgage because we have to charge more than you can afford."
Is that the kind of economy and is that the kind of system we live in? Is that what has become of Canada? Is that the level we are at in the House of Commons that we can find no way to rechannel some of that excess profit to provide mortgages for people at a price that they can afford? Is that the level to which we have fallen in the country? Is it now reasonable, is it acceptable, that some should be able to get a usurious return while others are forced out of their homes? Is that the level Canada has reached? I wonder. I wonder, and the government sits and tells me that, according to statistical analyses, things are getting better. Things are getting better! I dwell on the subject of banks because they are, in fact, the beneficiaries of all of this; but they are not the only beneficiaries. I want to make it clear that I understand that for large business there is a much better opportunity for absorbing the higher interest rates because they have access to money that small businesses or individual farmers do not. However, I want to say that I dwell on the subject of banks because we must start there.
It is impossible for a small business to carry the inventory necessary to remain in business at the kind of bridge financing costs that they now face. It is impossible, and we now know that. Do we do anything about it? No, we wring our hands and we walk away and say that statistically, things are getting better. But while we are walking away and while my relative is leaving his small business because it is impossible for him to survive-and I suspect that is true of the relatives and friends of others in the House-the Royal Bank has increased its assets by 79 per cent between 1977 and 1980. That is an increase in assets. However, while the farmer whom I know, who has been struggling for a number of years just to keep his head above water, working his heart out, trying to make sure that he maintains the family farm in order to provide the food that we have to eat, is putting off the purchase of machinery because he cannot afford the additional cost which is levied as the result of high interest rates, the Bank of Montreal increases its assets by the enormous amount of 110 per cent between 1977 and 1980.
I could go on with it because the Bank of Nova Scotia increased its profits by 100 per cent; the Imperial Bank of Commerce, by 85 per cent; the Toronto-Dominion Bank, by 91 per cent. We are not all suffering. We are not all suffering at all. I want to suggest that this House of Commons is not here to protect the banking interest. It is here to make it reasonable to do business in Canada. It is here for the purpose of writing laws which allow people to make reasonable profits. It is here also to represent the views of the 23-plus million Canadians who live in every part of this country and who, today, are asking, begging-they should be demanding-that we stop this nonsense and get on with dealing with what is fundamentally wrong with this economy.

May 14, 1981
The Economy
If it is true that the level of the Canadian dollar must fall, then the level of the Canadian dollar must fall! If the outcome of that is that imported products are more expensive, so be it. It is entirely possible, in fact it is probable, that Canadians might then buy Canadian-made products. This would increase the level of productivity and use up that 20-plus per cent of unused capacity that exists in Canada today and it would put more people to work and generate more goods.
When I asked a question today, the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) asked me, "Where is the market?" Mr. Speaker, there are markets and there are ways to do this. I say to the government and to the official opposition and to anyone else who cares to listen, that they will not be able to fulfil their mandate or meet their obligation to the people of Canada if they continue to allow the very soul of this nation to be undermined.
That soul is being undermined as a result of the difficulties that families now face when trying to meet even the minimal commitments that they have. It is an up-hill battle, which they are losing.
I suggest to the government that it stop this preoccupation with the level of the Canadian dollar and if need be, as my leader said earlier today, and as we have said a number of times-

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-EFFECTS OF HIGH INTEREST RATES AND DOUBLE-DIGIT INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that there is such a short time left to say the things I would like to say in a debate of this nature which deals with the government's shoddy economic performance at this time.
I was interested in the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans). He has learned well from the master. He knows how to take a lesson from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He does not have to be taught anything more. The Minister of Finance and the parliamentary secretary, and indeed, everyone who sits on the government benches, do not seem to care or to know what is happening to the hundreds and thousands of people across this country who are suffering day after day from the government's policies of high interest rates. They do not seem to know or care that there are a lot of people in this country who are in real need.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said that there are times that you have to forget about the trees and think only of the forest. He implied that they cannot afford to think of the individuals who are being hurt. I want to tell him that after you knock down all trees, there is no forest left. That is what we have to think about.
The Minister of Finance made some fatuous promises before the last election in an effort to be re-elected. As the result of those promises, the country is suffering now. Of course, the minister does not give that very much consideration. Safely out
of sight in the inner sanctum of the Department of Finance he can play with all sorts of ideas, many of which will bring further distress to Canadians. Remote as he is from real life, he can move from consideration of higher interest rates, which he has already forecast, to the introduction of wage and price controls or to the consideration of a tax-based incomes policy. He can do that while he is safely secluded in the penthouse of Place Bell Canada.
The minister has emerged from his quarters briefly to ask for suggestions. I want to give him one or two in the short time available to me. His comments of the last few days have shown how remote he is from the suffering that is going on across the country.
I want to suggest to the Minister of Finance that while he is contemplating which of the many complicated levers he will pull, he should set up a human misery index-something similar to the consumer price index-which he could read daily so that he could be aware of the hardship he has inflicted on Canadians. I could tell him that he will not be able to read that kind of index from some beach in Hawaii or from Kuwait, but he will be able to read it if he goes across the country talking to business people, farmers, and people living on fixed incomes in one community after the other.
Just the other day the minister accused us of pretending to be sympathetic to the plight of these people. There is no need to pretend about the suffering that is going on at the present time, Mr. Speaker. People are worried, upset, concerned and increasingly anxious. I want to give the minister an example of what is happening and of the kind of difficulties that Canadians find themselves in. I want to tell him about the case of one couple-one of many in my constituency-who have spoken to me. These people have been in the hotel business for a number of years. They worked hard and put their whole lives into it. Two years ago they decided to expand their business and do what many people in Kingston and The Islands have done, restore their building to its original form. They borrowed $650,000 from their friendly bank. The interest rate they obtained at that time was about 12 per cent; last week they were being charged 21 per cent. Their weekly interest payment is $3,000. The irony is that they are now taking in more money than they ever have in the history of their business, but they cannot meet their payments or do the things they want to do. They are being forced into bankruptcy. When they make their weekly deposit, the first thing the bank does is to take off the interest payment. They can meet that interest payment and the salaries of some 40 people but that is all. The cheques to their suppliers are being sent back marked "not sufficient funds".
Last week a cheque came back to them from Revenue Canada for $5,000. To add insult to injury, a $300 penalty was imposed by the very government that put them in this predicament in the first place because of high interest rates. They had applied for a small business development bond some five months ago but their application still has not been processed. They are still being hurt, week after week, by the government's high interest policies.
May 14, 1981

The other day I mentioned the mental anguish that people are suffering, and the minister laughed at me. It is that kind of mental anguish that this couple in Kingston is suffering. They are going through it because they do not know where the money will come from to pay their staff in the weeks ahead. They do not know whether they will have to lay them off and thus add another 40 people to the number of unemployed in this country. They do not know how they will be able to escape foreclosure or bankruptcy. They would rate very high on a human misery index if the minister were aware of what is happening to human beings in this country.
That is one suggestion that the minister could take into consideration and see if he cannot respond to the suffering that is going on in this country.

Mr. Speaker, in replying to a question on Tuesday of this week put by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated his confusion and ignorance of what is involved in applying to renew a mortgage. My colleague asked if the minister would honour his commitment to assist home owners who are having difficulty with the soaring interest rates. This commitment was made in March, 1980. The minister replied:
-because of the appreciation in the value of their homes they had experienced they were able to bear the burden of these increased mortgage payments. That is the fact.
Because an estimated 500,000 Canadians are renewing their mortgages at crippling interest rates, I sought to clarify the minister's statement on their behalf later in the question period. I suggested that when a Canadian home owner sits down with a mortgage officer and tells him that his home has appreciated, the mortgage officer is simply going to say "so have your mortgage payments". I would ask the minister how appreciation in the value of a home helps the Canadian home owner who has to make out-of-pocket mortgage payments. The minister replied:
Adjournment Debate
-if that is too complicated a concept for the hon. member to understand, I should like to draw his attention to a simpler concept-
The rest of his comments were nothing more than subterfuge, camouflage and confusion to cover the fact that he had no knowledge of the problem. Five hundred thousand Canadians are faced with increased mortgage payments as they renew their mortgages this year. Many are selling or abandoning their homes because they cannot afford the increased payment. A $40,000 mortgage loan at 10 per cent taken out in 1976 could be carried at $360 a month based upon a 25-year amortization. It now costs $590 a month to amortize $40,000 over 25 years at today's Liberal interest rates of 18 per cent. That is an increase of 61 per cent.
It is shocking that this crisis is facing the country. It is even more shocking that a minister of the Crown would confuse the Canadian people and then have the gall to suggest that the concept was too difficult for me to understand. For that reason I want to explain the facts of life to the Minister of Finance.
When a home appreciates in value, the home owner's equity increases. The home has become more valuable, but it does not put any more money in the home owner's pocket unless the house is sold. It does not mean that the mortgage principal is reduced. That can only be done by monthly payments which reduce the principal gradually, made out of the take-home pay of the home owner.
When home owners go to renew their mortgages, the mortgage officer considers the value of the home as security for the loan. If the home has appreciated, well and good. If it has depreciated, the mortgage officer must consider if the value is sufficient security to support the loan. However, the mortgage payments, usually monthly, on the renewed mortgage are another matter. The home owner must prove to the satisfaction of the mortgage officer that he, she or they can meet those payments out of their income or what we call take-home pay.
The point we were making is that increases in the mortgage interest rate from 10 per cent in 1976 to the current rate of 18 per cent as a result of the Liberal party's high interest rate policy result in an increase in the payment the home owner is making on a mortgage. If they can meet the payment, fine. If they cannot meet the payment, the home owner is in difficulty. The security, that is the increase in value which the minister thinks helps, goes by the board because the mortgage officer is only interested in how the home owner is going to make the payment. The mortgage company is then free to demand payment of the principal in full and the home owner seeks a mortgage elsewhere. It is absolute nonsense to suggest that appreciation in value helps to meet mortgage payments. It is unfair to the minister to hold out this hope to Canadian home owners.
I was tempted to pursue this matter as a question of privilege since the minister impugned my integrity and ability as a lawyer who practised real estate law for 11 years before entering politics by suggesting it was too complicated a matter for me to understand. Then I realized that the minister just did

May 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
not understand what was involved in renewing a mortgage. The minister is an embarrassment to the government. That concept was too complicated for him. I feel the minister will want to admit his error through his parliamentary secretary and apologize to the House and the Canadian people, and I hope his parliamentary secretary will have the dignity and integrity to do so on his behalf. Thank you very much.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, dealing with this problem of mortgage renewals, which is a very real problem, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) certainly has made a case. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) does not disagree with him one iota in respect of the problem and the fact that there is a problem. I think where the disagreement lies is in the extent of the problem and whether that problem can be coped with by the average Canadian home owner.
The majority of Canadian home owners renewing mortgages this year took out their mortgages in 1976. The average mortgage interest rate in 1976 was 11.8 per cent, or from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, and the current interest rate is about 18 per cent. This has resulted in an average increase in mortgage payments of some 40 per cent for those people who are renewing their mortgages. At the same time we have to ask whether they are able to meet these increased payments. We have shown here an unfortunate increase of 40 per cent in the payments necessary to service those mortgages.
However, in that same time period the average annual wage has increased by 55 per cent, some 15 percentage points more than the increase in the mortgage payments. The home owner is certainly not spending on average a greater proportion of his or her income on mortgage payments in 1981 than he did in 1976 when the mortgage was originally taken out.
At the same time it should be noted that the average house price has increased by some 48 per cent over the price paid in 1976. The hon. member for Simcoe North indicates that the minister did not understand when he said it was a complex problem, and perhaps the hon. member did not understand. In fact that is true because many of the people he is concerned about, and about whom we are concerned, are the lower income Canadians who bought homes at very high loan-to-val-ue ratios in 1976 and did so by not only taking out a first mortgage at 11.8 per cent, but a second mortgage at perhaps 14 per cent, and in some cases a third mortgage. Housing prices have gone up by 48 per cent, which means that the individual who had a first mortgage, a second mortgage, and, perhaps, in some cases a third mortgage in 1976, will be able to consolidate all those in a first mortgage. As a result, the figure I have given here, the 40 per cent increase, overstates the effect on the people we are concerned about here because a second mortgage at 13 per cent or 14 per cent would mean that payments were higher than indicated by an 11.8 per cent mortgage rate.
The fact of the matter is that the minister made an indication to the hon. member for Simcoe North, and the minister was right.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-I. REQUEST FOR ALLOCATION OF ADDITIONAL FUNDS. 2. PREPARATION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I directed a question yesterday to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) with regard to veterans' legislation. My question was as follows:
In light of the effect that new consumer price increases, rising energy prices and interest rates have on veterans and their families, as welt as the fact that over 2,000 applicants are having to wait up to two years for their pension appeals to be processed, will the Minister of Finance tell this House when he will be allocating the necessary funds so that the Minister of Veterans Affairs can bring in a bill providing some financial relief for veterans and their widows at this time of unprecedented need?
I received no assurance whatsoever from the Minister of Finance.
I posed a supplementary question which was answered by the parliamentary secretary to the acting minister of veterans affairs. Part of my question was the following:
There has been much speculation that legislation is now being prepared which would lower the phasing-in period for widows whose husbands were in receipt of less than a 48 per cent disability pension.
I received the assurance that this legislation will be brought in soon.
I also asked the government to launch an immediate inquiry into this backlog of 2,000 veteran pension applications which are taking up to two years to process. I called this a national disgrace, and I will call it a national disgrace again tonight.
The parliamentary secretary informed me that there are not 2,000 applications but approximately 1,200 applications in process. There is a conflict here. The Royal Canadian Legion has been keeping very close tabs on this. The legion is not in the habit of printing false information or exaggerated figures. I want to read from an editorial in the legion's magazine for May of 1981 which states:
In November, 1978, the chairman of the pension commission told a meeting of the standing committee on veterans affairs that the average length of time for a first application to reach a decision was 6 months, an improvement on the 7.8 months taken earlier. It was ... "almost back to normal."
It was stated at that time.
However, the average 7 months taken for a claim or 3'/2 months for a widow in December, 1979-
These are the commission's own statistics.
-has now climbed to more than 11 and 7 months respectively. A few cases will illustrate: 1. A May, 1980, request for a pension medical re-examination was completed July 30, 1980. The pertinent reports had not reached the commission's head office by February, 1981; the district office was awaiting additional information about the pensioned conditions. 2. An application for attendance allowance was submitted July 25, 1980, and acknowledged in September. The commission's request for investigation went forward to the medical examiner October 31,1980.
The veteran died in February.
I have statistics here for the last number of years which show that hundreds of veterans died before their pensions were processed. The legion's article also points out the following:
May 14, 1981

The number of appeals awaiting consideration by the pension review board hovers around 2,000. Now being heard are applications made two years ago. And the number of new appeals is increasing.
I suggest to the minister that he spend some time over at the Department of Veterans Affairs tracing some of these applications to find out why they are taking two years to be processed. I repeat again that this is an absolute disgrace.
The Royal Canadian Legion, Ontario Command helps many veterans with their applications. That command wrote to veterans and told them not to expect any action in a couple of months but that they will have to wait two years. This is the advice the Ontario Command gives to veterans in Ontario:
An assessment board, which due to several factors, will not be held any sooner than twelve to fourteen months, will only consider your condition as it was at the time of the Pension Medical Examination that the ruling was given for. In other words, when a board hears the claim it will be considering a ruling that by that time will be probably two years old.
That length of time is not acceptable, and we have heard nothing but excuses over the last number of years in this respect. The time has come for an end to excuses and for the minister to get over to that department and to find out what is going on there. I have in my hand a list of statistics respecting veterans who are dying before they receive their pension increases.
I have a letter here dated May 11, 1981, from Mr. J. Lamy, who is the dominion secretary of the Royal Canadian Legion. He points out in his letter:
-the delays in pension adjudications are of the utmost concern to us at this time.
Later in the paragraph, he says:
The situation is particularly bad in respect of first applications-
Further on in his letter he says:
We plan to present a brief to the standing committee-
I might say, whenever that is called.
I was very disappointed to read a speech which the parliamentary secretary gave recently to veterans in Peterborough in which I found some misleading information. The parliamentary secretary told the veterans in Peterborough the following:
It is a special pleasure to appear here and be able to assert that the federal government over the past year has improved the economic circumstances of many thousands of veterans and their survivors.
There are 2,000 veterans who have to wait two years to have their applications processed. Some are dying before the process is completed and their widows are having a rough time because of inflation, with the cost of gas having gone up 54 cents a gallon, and all the rest of it. I am sure hon. members know all the statistics, but then the parliamentary secretary tells them their economic lot is improving. That is not very good information to be handing out to veterans' organizations.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-I. REQUEST FOR ALLOCATION OF ADDITIONAL FUNDS. 2. PREPARATION OF AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate the House rules only allow me three minutes to respond to the distorted allegations made by the hon. member. However, I want to
Adjournment Debate
thank the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) for giving me the opportunity to clarify the situation respecting the delays and adjudications of applications for disability pensions made under the Pension Act.
There has been considerable talk recently about cases awaiting decisions. It is unfortunate but we must realize that the Pension Commission is unable to deal with all the applications it receives as soon as it would like. There have been some problems besetting the commission, and every effort is made to overcome them as quickly as possible.
At the first decision level, the commission has about 4,200 applications on hand. These cannot all be called backlog, some having been received only a few days ago. Because of the nature of the claims and the investigative work which must be done, it has never taken less than an average of five and a half months to deal with them. About 2,200 of these claims are less than five months old. The suggestion that there are 2,000 claims which will take two years to process, is simply not true.
The chairman of the commission has told me that their oldest claims at the first level are 21 months old and that there are only two in that category, and in both those cases they are waiting for information from another country.
Progress is being made in the time taken to process these applications. It now takes almost two months less on the average than it did at the end of 1980.
As far as the second level is concerned, that of the entitlement board appeal, the situation now is better than at any time in the commission's history. There are fewer than 900 cases to be heard across the country, in which the claimants have advised that they are ready to proceed, and the commission hears about 300 a month. This is less than half the number waiting to be heard a year ago.
In so far as proportionate pensions for widows are concerned, I believe it is well known that one of the acting minister's personal priorities is to try to improve the phasing-in time for widows of pensioners who, under present legislation, will have to wait for lengthy periods to receive their benefits. His success in this area will no doubt depend on the over-all financial picture.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-QUERY RESPECTING LEGISLATION AND COLLECTIVE BARGAINING RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question which I asked of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) on March 31, 1981, relating to the denial of the

May 14, 1981
Adjournment Debate
fundamental right to collective bargaining for members of the RCMP in Canada. At that time the Solicitor General indicated that amendments to the RCMP Act would be brought forward "soon". He stated that as far as most members of the force were concerned, there was a very effective system in effect for dealing with industrial relations within the force.
In the few minutes I have this evening, I would like to point out that the minister promised on many occasions to bring forward this important piece of legislation affecting members of the RCMP right across the country. In the Speech from the Throne, there was a promise that the RCMP legislation would be amended. In May of 1980, the minister agreed that the present disciplinary procedures were unfair. He said that legislation was a high priority and would be brought forward very soon. He repeated that promise on a number of occasions. In the fall of 1980, he stated that legislation would be brought forward within a month. Again on February 23, 1981, in Edmonton the Solicitor General stated that this legislation was a priority for the government and that it would be brought forward within a month. We see very clearly that on many occasions the minister promised to bring forward this important legislation, but to this day we have not seen any results whatsoever.
Perhaps this reflects the lack of clout of the minister in cabinet. One could only hope that in the very near future members of the RCMP would at long last have an adequate mechanism set out in the RCMP Act.
There are several concerns of the force, but the fundamental one is its right to full collective bargaining without the right to strike. They recognize that the right to strike is one they do not wish to receive at this point. They are prepared to have differences settled by arbitration. The right to full collective bargaining and freedom of association should be accorded to members of the RCMP.
In my question on March 31,1 pointed out that the freedom of association supposedly granted to all Canadians under the charter of rights in fact is denied to members of the RCMP. On other occasions I have noted in the House that that same freedom of association is denied to employees of Parliament, including members of the security staff on the Hill. What is the effect of this denial of collective bargaining rights? This has meant that the conditions of members of the RCMP in terms of pay and their relative standard has been falling further and further behind. It is the only major police force in Canada which does not have collective bargaining rights. The pay and working conditions of the RCMP have been steadily declining.
The Solicitor General said that there is a system of divisional representatives. Members of the force acknowledge that this simply is not working. The divisional representatives must represent literally hundreds of members and cannot bargain on pay. The bargaining process for pay is a mystery. What the Treasury Board is prepared to offer and what senior members of the force are seeking are mysteries. There is no recognition of the increased costs facing members of the force in certain areas of the country such as my own area in British Columbia.
One effect of this is that senior members are leaving the force and are being replaced by recruits. Of course this has a very serious impact, particularly in areas such as Burnaby and Surrey which are training detachments.
A number of other concerns face the force at this point. They include the fact that the multimillion dollar pension scheme has no significant involvement of members of the force. Surely this must be changed. They are concerned about certain aspects of working conditions. They believe they need improved weapons and ammunition. They are concerned that soft body armour should be issued as well. They are disturbed at the arbitrary dismissal of their request for night sticks by the commissioner's office. They insist that the vacancies which presently occur in a number of detachments-vacant staff positions which result in staff shortages-jeopardize in some cases the safety not only of members of the RCMP but of members of the public. They insist these vacancies must be filled.
It is clear the government has failed to live up to its commitment to members of the RCMP. It took a recent court decision in the federal court to permit members of the RCMP to be represented in disciplinary proceedings by a lawyer. This was a court proceeding initiated by the association of 17 divisions. It was not until that decision-and I understand fortunately the decision is not being appealed-that this fundamental right to counsel was accorded to members of the RCMP in internal disciplinary proceedings.
The concern that I wish to raise this evening, and which I have raised on other occasions, is that the level of frustration within the RCMP is steadily increasing as their pay falls further and further behind. As I said, they want the right to full collective bargaining, a right which is accorded to all other major police forces in Canada. The Solicitor General has refused to act on this right. We will be looking with great interest at the proposed legislation with regard to the RCMP to ensure that it does accord the right to collective bargaining.
To conclude, we will be pursuing the matters which I have raised, including vacancies in various detachments, the concern about the pension plan and working conditions and, most important, the widening gulf in pay as compared with other police forces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-QUERY RESPECTING LEGISLATION AND COLLECTIVE BARGAINING RIGHTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was glad to note from the concluding remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) that he retains the faith that the RCMP bill will be forthcoming. In fact, I had hoped that it would long since have been tabled in the House. I can tell the House that I am still working on that legislation. It is still very much in the works and I hope it will be tabled very soon.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-QUERY RESPECTING LEGISLATION AND COLLECTIVE BARGAINING RIGHTS
speechtext: You have been saying that for a year.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-QUERY RESPECTING LEGISLATION AND COLLECTIVE BARGAINING RIGHTS
speechtext:
I concede that. I had hoped that I would have been able to bring it forward some time ago. It has not been a
May 14, 1981

matter of clout but a matter of other legislation before the House and other legislation which is in the hands of legislative draftsmen. But the way is now clear for moving it forward. Today I saw material associated with the legislation. I do not claim full responsibility for the long delay which has taken place since the Marin commission in 1976 made the recommendations which led to the commitment of the government to introduce legislation. The Marin commission recommended an improved procedure for complaints from the public and, of equal importance, more formal grievance procedures for individual members of the force. This will permit individual members of the force the right to counsel, and many other advantages in their industrial relations with the force and issues of discipline which are long overdue.
1 am glad that the hon. member acknowledges that this legislation will be coming. I hope he will be happy with it. But the legislation will not change, as he indicated he hoped it might, the right to collective bargaining. As the hon. member
Adjournment Debate
put it, there is no fundamental right to full collective bargaining in Canadian society. That is a right which Parliament has accorded within the public service. It is something the Pearson government did. It is not a right which has been extended to all units of the public service, as the hon. member indicated. It was not accorded to the Armed Forces, the RCMP, the staff of the House of Commons or to others. He can consult the debates at that time and the discussions in committee for all of the reasons put forward for not according this collective bargaining right. I think the reasons were good ones and they still apply. I refute his claim that he speaks for the force when he says that there is a broadly-based feeling that there should be the right to collective bargaining. There is a divisional representation system which is an effective one.
